Let $(V,\tau,g,A)$ be as in [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] and let $(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ and $(o',u',(e_1',e_2',e_3'))$ be two adapted charts, with coordinate functions $(t,x)$ and $(t',x')$ of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]].

1. There are $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,v\in\mathbb R^3$ and a matrix $R\in O(3)$ such that for every $p\in A$

$$t'(p)=t(p)+b,\qquad x'(p)=R\,x(p)+v\,t(p)+a.$$

If $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(e_1',e_2',e_3')$ are both positively oriented for the fixed orientation of $K$, then $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]).

2. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be a map whose first-chart time coordinate satisfies $t(\gamma(s))=s$ for all $s\in I$. Write $x(s):=x(\gamma(s))$ and $y(s):=x'(\gamma(s))$. The regularity hypothesis below means that this coordinate function $x:I\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuously differentiable (respectively, twice continuously differentiable); no additional smooth structure on $A$ is assumed. If $x$ is continuously differentiable then $y$ is continuously differentiable with

$$y'(s)=R\,x'(s)+v\qquad(s\in I),$$

and if $x$ is twice continuously differentiable then $y''(s)=R\,x''(s)$ for all $s\in I$. Equivalently, in the differentiated variables of the two charts, $dx'/dt'=R\,dx/dt+v$ and $d^2x'/dt'^2=R\,d^2x/dt^2$.

3. Consequently $x''=0$ on $I$ if and only if $y''=0$ on $I$: the two charts agree on which time-parametrized curves have zero coordinate acceleration.

In the notation of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]:

1. $I_3\in SO(3)$, and for all $R,S\in SO(3)$ the matrices $RS$ and $R^{\mathsf T}$ again lie in $SO(3)$; moreover $\det R=1$, $R$ is invertible, and its inverse is $R^{\mathsf T}$, so also $RR^{\mathsf T}=I_3$.
2. Consequently $SO(3)$ is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]], [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]).

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the set of $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb R$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), with identity $I_3$ and product as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], transpose $R^{\mathsf T}$ as in [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and determinant $\det R$ as in [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].

The **orthogonal group** and the **special orthogonal group** are the subsets

$$O(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\},\qquad SO(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\ \text{and}\ \det R=1\}.$$

Equivalently $SO(3)=O(3)\cap\{R:\det R=1\}$. Elements of $SO(3)$ are called **rotations**. The identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with the function space $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ is the one of [[def-matrix-space]]; when $M_3(\mathbb R)$ is regarded as a metric or topological space, this is always the Euclidean metric of that identification.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about particles and their motion, in the spacetime of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and the frames of [[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Particle labels and worldlines.** A model of the framework has **particle
labels** $i=1,\dots,N$ for some $N\ge1$. To each label and each *inertial
frame* of the model — an adapted chart $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ with
coordinates $(t,x)$ in the sense of [[post-cm01-frames]] — there is assigned a
**worldline** $\gamma_{i}:I\to A$ described in that frame, where
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval — that is, an interval
of the form $(a,b)$ with $-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points —
the curve $\gamma_{i}$ is of class $C^{2}$ in the adapted coordinates of the frame,
and the **parameter condition**

$$\tau\bigl(\gamma_{i}(t)-o\bigr)=t\qquad(t\in I)$$

holds: the curve parameter is the elapsed time from the origin of the frame, so
in the frame's coordinates $\gamma_{i}(t)=(t,x_{i}(t))$ with
$x_{i}:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$. The parameter condition replaces
the causal conditions of relativistic kinematics: no timelike condition on the
velocity and no upper bound on its Euclidean norm is imposed, and the
parameter is not free up to reparametrization.

**(ii) Description in another frame.** The same motion described in a second
inertial frame is the curve obtained by the time reparametrization of the two
frames: if $(t',x')$ are the coordinates of the second frame and
$t'=t+b$ is the time component of the transformation between the two frames
([[post-cm01-frames]], [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]),
then the description of the motion in the second frame is the curve
$\gamma_{i,b}(t'):=\gamma_{i}(t'-b)$, defined on $I+b$, and it again satisfies
the parameter condition $\tau(\gamma_{i,b}(t')-o')=t'$ with respect to the
second frame's origin $o'$. This is a consistency requirement of the model's
frame language; the accompanying spatial transformation of the coordinate
curve is the affine law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]],
and its kinematic consequences are proved in [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(iii) Regularity is frame-independent.** The class of the worldline is
independent of the frame used to describe it: by the transformation law of
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], the coordinates of the
same event in two inertial frames differ by
$t'=t+b$, $x'=Rx+vt+a$ with constant $b,a,v$ and $R\in SO(3)$, so a coordinate
curve is twice continuously differentiable in one inertial frame exactly when
its reparametrized description is twice continuously differentiable in the
other. The assumptions of this postulate are therefore read in any one inertial
frame without loss.

**(iv) Velocity and acceleration.** In a fixed inertial frame the quantities
$w_{i}:=dx_{i}/dt$ and $a_{i}:=d^{2}x_{i}/dt^{2}$ are the **coordinate
velocity** and **coordinate acceleration** of the label, of dimensions
$\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ by [[def-cm01-units]]; they are defined
precisely, and their transformation under a change of inertial frame is
recorded, in [[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]].

**(v) Fixed inertial mass.** Each particle label $i$ carries a **mass**
$m_{i}>0$, a primitive parameter of the model with dimension $\mu$
([[def-cm01-units]]). The mass is fixed: it is the same positive number at all
times and in all inertial frames of this model; the index $i$ identifies a label within that model and asserts no cross-model identification or equality of mass parameters. It
is not a function of the time coordinate, of the position or of the velocity,
and no variable-mass model is a model of this clause. The mass enters the
dynamics only through its later appearance in the equation of motion; this
postulate attaches no dynamics to it. Distinct labels may carry distinct
masses, and the masses are model data, not measured values.

**(vi) Point-particle idealization.** The model retains of each label only its
position and its fixed mass, together with the label index: size, shape, spin,
deformation, temperature and internal degrees of freedom are omitted, and the
quantity $x_{i}(t)$ is the single point representing the label at time $t$. An
application of the model must state when this idealization is adequate for the
system at hand; for a body whose rotation, deformation or internal structure
matters for the question asked, the point-particle model is not adequate and a
richer model must be specified. The framework makes no claim that every
physical body is a point particle.

**(vii) Calibration caveat.** An apparatus calibration may *estimate* a mass
parameter of a concrete body under a stated measurement model, with its
assumptions, sampling and uncertainty; such an estimate neither defines the
mass parameter of a label nor verifies the equation of motion in which it
occurs, and it is not deduced from this postulate. No measured value of any
mass is asserted by this item.

Let an inertial frame $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ be fixed, and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be the worldline of a
particle label described in this frame as in [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; thus
$\gamma$ is of class $C^{2}$, parametrized so that $t(\gamma(s))=s$ for all
$s\in I$, and

$$\gamma(s)=o+su+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\xi_{j}(s)\,e_{j}$$

for the unique coordinate functions $\xi_{j}:I\to\mathbb R$ of the point
$\gamma(s)$ in the adapted chart ([[def-cm-affine-time-space]],
[[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]]).

**(a) The coordinate curve.** The **coordinate curve** of $\gamma$ in the
frame is

$$x_{\gamma}:=\bigl(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3}\bigr):I\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3}.$$

It is of class $C^{2}$ by the regularity clause of [[post-cm01-worldlines]],
and it determines $\gamma$ by the display above, since the parameter condition
fixes the time coordinate. It has dimension $[\,\xi_{j}\,]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(b) Coordinate velocity and acceleration.** The **derivative** of a
vector-valued map is taken componentwise: for the map $x_{\gamma}$ above, its
derivative at $s$ is

$$x_{\gamma}'(s):=\bigl(\xi_{1}'(s),\xi_{2}'(s),\xi_{3}'(s)\bigr),$$

where each $\xi_{j}'(s)=\lim_{h\to0}\bigl(\xi_{j}(s+h)-\xi_{j}(s)\bigr)/h$ is
the ordinary derivative of a real function. The **coordinate velocity** of the
label in the frame is

$$w(s):=x_{\gamma}'(s)\in\mathbb R^{3},$$

with components $w_{j}=\xi_{j}'$, and the **coordinate acceleration** is the
coordinate velocity of the velocity,

$$a(s):=w'(s)=x_{\gamma}''(s)\in\mathbb R^{3}.$$

Their dimensions are $[w_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[a_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-2}$, read
in metres per second and metres per second squared. The triple $w(s)$ is the
triple of numbers read in the frame's axes: it is a coordinate description,
not an element of spacetime.

**(c) Spatial velocity and acceleration vectors.** For the affine curve
$\gamma:I\to A$, subtraction of events uses the affine displacement in $V$.
Define its derivative by the limit in the finite-dimensional vector space
$V$,
$$\gamma'(s):=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\gamma(s+h)-\gamma(s)}{h}=u+\sum_j\xi_j'(s)e_j,$$
and define $\gamma''(s)$ as the derivative of the $V$-valued map
$\gamma'$. This is the canonical identification of each affine tangent
space with $V$; the $C^2$ coordinate regularity guarantees both limits.
The frame's time direction
$u$ and spatial basis identify two elements of the spatial displacement space
$K$ attached to the motion:

$$\underline{v}(s):=\gamma'(s)-u=\sum_{j=1}^{3}w_{j}(s)\,e_{j}\in K,\qquad \underline{a}(s):=\gamma''(s)=\sum_{j=1}^{3}a_{j}(s)\,e_{j}\in K.$$

Here $\gamma'(s)-u$ indeed lies in $K=\ker\tau$, because $\tau(\gamma'(s))=\frac{d}{ds}\tau(\gamma(s)-o)=1$ by linearity of $\tau$ and the parameter condition. The vectors $\underline{v}(s)$ and $\underline{a}(s)$ are the **spatial velocity vector** and **spatial acceleration vector** of the label in the frame; the velocity depends on the frame time direction $u$, whereas the acceleration is an intrinsic element of $K$ unchanged by an inertial frame change (time shifts have derivative $1$). Their coordinates in the frame's basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ are the triples $w(s)$ and $a(s)$.

**(d) Speed.** The **speed** of the label in the frame at time $s$ is the
Euclidean norm $\|w(s)\|_{2}=\sqrt{\sum_{j}w_{j}(s)^{2}}$, of dimension
$\ell\tau^{-1}$; equivalently $\|\underline{v}(s)\|_{2}=\sqrt{g(\underline{v}(s),\underline{v}(s))}$,
the norm induced by the spatial metric, since the basis is $g$-orthonormal.

**(e) Transformation under a change of inertial frame (recorded).** Let a
second inertial frame be given, with coordinates $(t',x')$ and transformation
parameters $(b,a,v,R)$ as in [[post-cm01-frames]], and let
$\eta(t'):=x'(\gamma(t'-b))\in\mathbb R^{3}$ be the description of the motion
in the second frame. Then

$$\eta'(t')=R\,w(t'-b)+v,\qquad \eta''(t')=R\,a(t'-b),$$

that is, in the differentiated variables and abbreviated notation
$w'=Rw+v$ and $a'=Ra$. This law is clause 2 of the mathematical transformation
law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], recorded here
in the model's notation; the definition itself asserts neither law. The
model-level statement of the law, including the frame-independence of the
property $a\equiv0$, is proved as a theorem later on this page.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: By clause 1 of [L1] applied to the two adapted charts $F,F'$, there are $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in O(3)$ with $t'(p)=t(p)+b$ and $x'(p)=Rx(p)+vt(p)+a_{0}$ for all $p\in A$; both bases of an inertial frame are positively oriented by definition, so the orientation clause of [L1] gives $R\in SO(3)$; this proves clause 1.

For the composition, apply $G(b_{1},a_{1},v_{1},R_{1})$ and then $G(b_{2},a_{2},v_{2},R_{2})$ to a point $(t,x)$: the intermediate point is $(s,y)=(t+b_{1},\,R_{1}x+v_{1}t+a_{1})$, and the final point is $(s+b_{2},\,R_{2}y+v_{2}s+a_{2})=\bigl(t+b_{1}+b_{2},\ R_{2}R_{1}x+(R_{2}v_{1}+v_{2})t+R_{2}a_{1}+v_{2}b_{1}+a_{2}\bigr)$, which is the displayed composite by associativity of matrix multiplication and bilinearity of the matrix–vector product.

For the inverse, let $(s,y)=G(b,a_{0},v,R)(t,x)$ with $R\in SO(3)$. Then $t=s-b$ and $x=R^{-1}(y-vt-a_{0})=R^{\mathsf T}\bigl(y-v(s-b)-a_{0}\bigr)=R^{\mathsf T}y-R^{\mathsf T}v\,s+R^{\mathsf T}(vb-a_{0})$, so the inverse map is $(s,y)\mapsto\bigl(s-b,\ R^{\mathsf T}y+(-R^{\mathsf T}v)s+R^{\mathsf T}(vb-a_{0})\bigr)$, the displayed transformation, and substituting it into the forward transformation returns $(s,y)$.

By [L3], $t(\gamma(s))=s$ for all $s\in I$; hence $t'(\gamma(s))=s+b$ by step 1.1, and substituting $p=\gamma(s)$ into the second display of step 1.1 gives $x'(\gamma(s))=Rx(s)+vs+a_{0}$ for all $s\in I$.

In the composites of steps 1.2 and 1.3 the rotation parameters are $R_{2}R_{1}$ and $R^{\mathsf T}$, both in $SO(3)$ by [L2], and the other parameters lie in $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R^{3}$; the identity transformation $G(0,0,0,I_{3})$ is present, so the set of Galilean transformations is closed under composition and inversion and the frame-change relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; this proves clause 4.

Define $\eta(t'):=x'(\gamma(t'-b))$ on $I+b$ as in [L4]. By step 2.1, $\eta(s+b)=x'(\gamma(s))=Rx(s)+vs+a_{0}$, so substituting $s=t'-b$ gives $\eta(t')=Rx(t'-b)+v(t'-b)+a_{0}$ there; a composition of the $C^{2}$ curve $x$ with the affine map $t'\mapsto t'-b$ is $C^{2}$, so $\eta$ is of class $C^{2}$, and differentiating the display with the chain rule [L5], whose inner derivative is $1$, gives $\eta'(t')=Rx'(t'-b)+v=Rw(t'-b)+v$ and $\eta''(t')=Rx''(t'-b)=Ra(t'-b)$; this proves clause 2.

If $a\equiv0$ on $I$, then $\eta''(t')=Ra(t'-b)=0$ for every $t'\in I+b$ by step 3.1; conversely, if $\eta''\equiv0$ on $I+b$, then for every $s\in I$ step 3.1 gives $Ra(s)=\eta''(s+b)=0$, and multiplying by $R^{\mathsf T}$ on the left and using $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3}$ from [L2] gives $a(s)=R^{\mathsf T}\eta''(s+b)=0$; this proves clause 3.

boundaries.evidence: The domain $I$ is a nondegenerate interval by [L3], so the empty case is excluded by hypothesis; step 2.1 applies the parameter condition at every $s\in I$.
Zero parameters are allowed and covered: step 1.1 admits $b=0$, $a_{0}=0$, $v=0$, $R=I_{3}$, and steps 1.2-4.1 remain valid, reducing to the identity transformation.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is stated for one worldline and one ordered pair of inertial frames; there is no indexed family whose length-one case could be special.

boundaries.evidence: Degenerate configurations of the statement are the identity transformation and the case $R=I_{3}$ with nonzero $b,a_{0},v$; step 1.1 includes both, and the composition and inverse formulas of steps 1.2-1.3 are evaluated there.
$I$ and $I+b$ are open intervals, so no endpoint is evaluated; step 3.1 differentiates the coordinate expression on $I+b$, every point of which is interior.

boundaries.reason: The parameters $(b,a_{0},v,R)$ are determined by the two charts and the proof selects nothing from any family; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: Forward direction of clause 3: step 4.1 derives $\eta''\equiv0$ from $a\equiv0$ via $\eta''=Ra$.
Reverse direction of clause 3: step 4.1 derives $a\equiv0$ from $\eta''\equiv0$ by left multiplication with $R^{\mathsf T}$.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked steps 1.1-4.1 and exact current transition lemma. Both frames are given adapted charts with positive orientation, so R belongs to SO(3). Time reparametrization is a bijection I+b to I with derivative 1. Eta=Rx(tprime-b)+v(tprime-b)+a0 is C2; both directions of zero acceleration use Rtranspose R=I. Composition has translation R2 a1+v2 b1+a2 and boost R2 v1+v2; inverse parameters -b, Rtranspose(vb-a0), -Rtranspose v, Rtranspose satisfy both inverse identities. Associativity is inherited from function composition. Affineness for zero second derivative follows componentwise by zero-derivative constancy on an interval. Cases zero boost/translation/time shift and identity rotation included. Conditional on the given frames; no unproved existence of a frame, dynamics or empirical claim is used.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the non-relativistic classical mechanics framework the following statements about spacetime.

**(i) Spacetime data.** Spacetime is the mathematical structure
$(V,\tau,g,A,\text{fixed orientation of }K)$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]]: a
four-dimensional real vector space $V$; a surjective linear map
$\tau:V\to\mathbb R$, the **absolute-time covector**; the kernel
$K=\ker\tau$, a three-dimensional real vector space, the **spatial displacement
space**; a **spatial metric** $g$, a symmetric positive-definite bilinear form
$g:K\times K\to\mathbb R$; a fixed **orientation** of $K$, that is, a chosen one
of the two classes of ordered bases of $K$ under the equivalence generated by
positive-determinant changes of basis; and an affine space $A$ modelled on $V$
(a nonempty set with a free and transitive $V$-action, with displacements as in
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]]). The elements of $A$ are the **events** of the
model. The structure is the arena of the model; no equation of motion, force
law or matter content is asserted by this clause.

**(ii) Interpretation of the data.** For a displacement $w\in V$, the number
$\tau(w)$ is the **elapsed time** carried by $w$, read in seconds; for a
displacement $k\in K$ inside a simultaneous slice, the number $g(k,k)$ is the
**squared spatial length** of $k$, read in square metres; the square root
$\sqrt{g(k,k)}$ is the length of $k$. The dimensions and units are those fixed
by [[def-cm01-units]], so that $[\tau(w)]=\tau$ and $[g(k,k)]=\ell^{2}$. The
orientation of $K$ is the convention relative to which spatial bases are called
positively oriented and against which orientation-preserving rotations are
defined.

**(iii) Absolute time, simultaneity and distance.** Two events $p,q\in A$ are
**simultaneous** when their displacement lies in $K$, that is, when
$\tau(q-p)=0$. Simultaneity is an equivalence relation on $A$: it is reflexive
because $\tau(0)=0$, symmetric because $\tau(p-q)=-\tau(q-p)$ and transitive
because $\tau$ is additive. Its classes are the **simultaneous slices**
$A_{t}=\{p\in A:\tau(p-o)=t\}$ of any adapted chart; the class does not depend
on the choice of adapted chart, and the elapsed time between two events is the
chart-independent number $\tau(q-p)$. Two events of a common slice carry the
**slice distance** $d_{g}(p,q):=\sqrt{g(p-q,p-q)}$, which is defined because
$p-q\in K$; distances are not defined across distinct slices by this structure.

**(iv) Smooth structure.** $A$ is read with the affine smooth structure
determined by its affine coordinates: an adapted chart of
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]] is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}$
whose inverse is the map $(t,x)\mapsto o+tu+\sum_{i}x_{i}e_{i}$, and curves are
declared $C^{k}$ when their coordinate functions in one (equivalently, every)
adapted chart are $C^{k}$. The equivalence of the two readings is supplied by
the affine transition law between adapted charts proved in
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]; this postulate adopts
the resulting smooth structure as the one in which regularity of worldlines and
of force maps is stated.

**(v) What the structure excludes.** The data contain no inner product on $V$,
no Lorentzian metric, no light cone, no universal speed bound, no null cones
and no causal classification of displacements other than the split into
$\tau$-values; they contain no distinguished origin, no distinguished vector
$u$ with $\tau(u)=1$ and no distinguished basis of $K$. Consequently the
structure by itself distinguishes no inertial frame: the class of frames and
the transformations between them are fixed separately, by the frame postulate
[[post-cm01-frames]]. No statement about the speed of any signal, about
electromagnetic propagation or about gravitation is made here.

**(vi) Status.** These clauses are adopted assumptions of the model, not
theorems and not empirical findings. They are not derived from the uniqueness
theory of differential equations, from any symmetry principle or from
experiment; the Newtonian tradition and Galilean relativity motivate them. The
model makes no claim that the physical world is exactly a four-dimensional
affine space with these data, and no numerical measurement is recorded.

Let $V$ be a real vector space of dimension $4$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let $\tau:V\to\mathbb R$ be a surjective linear map ([[def-linear-map]]). Put

$$K:=\ker\tau=\{v\in V:\tau(v)=0\},$$

the kernel of $\tau$ ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]). The kernel is a linear subspace ([[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]]), so the quotient vector space $V/K$ is defined ([[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]]). The first isomorphism theorem gives the linear isomorphism $V/K\to\operatorname{im}\tau=\mathbb R$, $v+K\mapsto\tau(v)$ ([[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-for-vector-spaces]]). Since $\mathbb R$ has the one-element standard basis, $\dim\mathbb R=1$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] with $F=\mathbb R$ and $n=1$); rank-nullity for the surjective map $\tau$ therefore gives $\dim K=4-1=3$ ([[thm-rank-nullity]]).

Let $g$ be an inner product on $K$ in the sense of [[def-inner-product-space]]: a symmetric positive definite $\mathbb R$-bilinear form $g:K\times K\to\mathbb R$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set equipped with an action of the additive group of $V$, written $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$, that is free and transitive: explicitly, $(p+v)+w=p+(v+w)$ and $p+0=p$ for all $p\in A$ and $v,w\in V$, and for all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $p+v=q$; write $q-p$ for that unique vector. The identities $p+(q-p)=q$, $(q-p)+(r-q)=r-p$ and $q-p=-(p-q)$ follow from the axioms together with uniqueness of the displacement. Such a set is an **affine space modelled on $V$**, and its elements are **events**. (This formulation restates the affine-space structure used here so that the item is self-contained; the general theory of affine spaces is supplied by the special-relativity collection for its own consumers.)

Fix an orientation of $K$ in the sense of [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]; this is a chosen orientation class, not a chosen spatial basis.

An **adapted chart** for the data $(V,\tau,g,A)$ is a triple $(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ consisting of

1. an origin $o\in A$;
2. a vector $u\in V$ with $\tau(u)=1$;
3. an ordered basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $K$ that is $g$-orthonormal and positively oriented with respect to the fixed orientation of $K$ ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]], [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

An adapted chart exists for every such set of data and fixed orientation, by clause 3 of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]].

For spatial coordinate vectors $x\in\mathbb R^3$, this item uses the one-based labels $x_i:=x(i-1)$ for $1\le i\le3$; thus $(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ lists the values at $0,1,2$ of the function-space vector of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The labels $e_1,e_2,e_3$ name the corresponding ordered spatial basis; they do not change the underlying index set of $\mathbb R^3$.

The **adapted coordinates** of a point $p\in A$ in this chart are the pair $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ determined by

$$p=o+tu+\sum_{i=1}^{3}x_ie_i,$$

when such a pair exists (existence and uniqueness are [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]], so that the notation is defined for every $p$). The number $t$ is the **time coordinate** and $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ the **spatial coordinate vector** of $p$ in the chart. When $K$ is identified with $\mathbb R^3$ through the coordinates in $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, the assignment $p\mapsto(t,x)$ is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$.

**Simultaneous slices.** For $t\in\mathbb R$ set

$$A_t:=\{p\in A:\tau(p-o)=t\}.$$

The family $\{A_t\}_{t\in\mathbb R}$ is the family of **simultaneous slices** of the chart. Each $A_t$ is an affine space modelled on $K$; the derivation is immediate from the affine identities and linearity of $\tau$ and is recorded in [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]]. The **slice distance** of two points $p,q$ in a common slice $A_t$ is

$$d_g(p,q):=\sqrt{g(p-q,\,p-q)},$$

the square root taken in $\mathbb R$; this is defined because $p-q\in K$ for points of a common slice. In adapted coordinates $d_g(p,q)=\|x(p)-x(q)\|_2$, with $\|\cdot\|_2$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about frames, in the spacetime structure of [[post-cm01-spacetime]].

**(i) Rotations.** A **rotation** is a matrix $R\in SO(3)$, where

$$SO(3)=\left\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3},\ \det R=1\right\}$$

in the sense of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A rotation acts on spatial
column vectors by matrix multiplication; its entries are dimensionless under
the radian convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Rotations are part of the
formulation of spatial changes of basis; the definition of $SO(3)$ itself
asserts nothing about physical space.

**(ii) Inertial frames.** An **inertial frame** is the global adapted affine
chart of the spacetime data determined by

$$o\in A,\qquad u\in V\ \text{with}\ \tau(u)=1,\qquad (e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\ \text{an ordered,}\ g\text{-orthonormal, positively oriented basis of }K,$$

with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ as in [[def-cm-affine-time-space]]: the time
coordinate is $t(p)=\tau(p-o)$ and the spatial coordinates are the coefficients
of $p-o-tu\in K$ in the basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$. Existence and uniqueness
of the coordinates, and the affine structure of the slices, are the mathematical
content of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]] and
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]]; no physical claim beyond the reading of clause
(iii) is attached to them here.

An inertial frame is a **coordinate chart**: the triple $(o,u,(e_{i}))$. It is
definitively not an observer congruence and not a time-varying basis field. In
the model the basis $(e_{i})$ is fixed once and for all; a family of bases
depending on the time coordinate is a different structure, whose kinematics is
defined separately where it is used, and is not an inertial frame. The physical
reading of the frame is that $t$ is the model's time coordinate in seconds and
$x$ the spatial position in metres, by the conventions of
[[def-cm01-units]].

**(iii) Stationary observers.** For $x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ the curve
$\alpha_{x_{0}}:\mathbb R\to A$, $\alpha_{x_{0}}(t):=o+tu+\sum_{j=1}^{3}(x_{0})_{j}e_{j}$,
is the **observer at rest in the frame at position $x_{0}$**; the family
$\{\alpha_{x_{0}}\}_{x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}}$ is the **stationary observer
congruence** of the frame. Each curve has $t(\alpha_{x_{0}}(s))=s$, is
$C^{\infty}$ in adapted coordinates, and in the frame's own spatial
coordinates has constant coordinate triple $x_{0}$. Here an **observer
worldline** means precisely a $C^2$ curve $\alpha:I\to A$ on a nondegenerate
open real interval with $t(\alpha(s))=s$, used to describe an observer; the
stationary curves just defined have $I=\mathbb R$. This kinematic definition
assigns neither a particle label nor a mass or a dynamical law to an observer.
A particle worldline will separately be assigned to a particle label in the
particle postulate. The congruence is a derived object, determined by the frame and the spacetime data, not an additional primitive. Distinct frames can have the same family of parametrized curves: if $o' = o+\sum_jc_je_j$ while $u'=u$ and $e_j'=e_j$, then $\alpha'_{x_0}(t)=\alpha_{x_0+c}(t)$ for all $t$. Thus shifting only the spatial origin relabels this family. Changing $u$ changes the curve family, since every curve in it has the affine derivative $u$.

**(iv) Allowed changes between frames.** The model adopts the class of
transformations between inertial frames

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x'=Rx+vt+a,$$

where $b\in\mathbb R$ is a **time shift** ($[b]=\tau$), $a\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a
**spatial translation** ($[a_{i}]=\ell$), $v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a **boost
velocity** ($[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$) and $R\in SO(3)$ a **rotation**
($[R_{ij}]=1$). Every pair of inertial frames is related by exactly one such
transformation: that two adapted charts of the same data differ by a
transformation of this form, with $R\in SO(3)$ because both bases are
positively oriented, is the mathematical transformation law proved in
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]. Uniqueness follows by comparing the coordinate maps on all $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$: evaluating the time map fixes $b$; evaluating the spatial map at $(0,0)$ fixes $a$, at $(1,0)$ fixes $v$, and at $(0,e_j)$ for the three standard coordinate vectors fixes each column of $R$. The kinematic
consequences of the law — the transformation of coordinate velocity and
acceleration, and the frame-independence of zero coordinate acceleration — are
proved as a statement about the model in
[[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(v) Free motion is not asserted here.** The framework's dynamics enters
through the force and equation-of-motion postulates of the pages that follow;
those pages adopt, as the content of Newton's first law, that there exist
inertial frames in the sense of clause (ii) in which a particle with zero
applied interaction has zero coordinate acceleration. This postulate
introduces the frames and their changes but asserts no dynamics: it does not
state that any particular motion has zero acceleration, and it does not
privilege any one inertial frame — each of them is a legitimate arena for the
formulation of the model's equations.

**(vi) Kinematic symmetry is not conservation.** The class (iv) is a class of
coordinate changes. A quantity is **conserved along a motion** when its value as a function of the frame time is constant on the interval of that motion. No such constancy is asserted here, nor is it asserted that every
mechanical system's description is invariant in form; a force law must also
transform appropriately under (iv) to be a law of the model in every frame, and
an external apparatus or background field can single out frames for the
description of a concrete experiment. Conservation statements, when they hold,
are theorems of later pages with their own hypotheses, not consequences of
this postulate.

Adopt the spacetime assumptions of [[post-cm01-spacetime]], the frame
assumptions of [[post-cm01-frames]] and the worldline assumptions of
[[post-cm01-worldlines]]. Let

$$F=\bigl(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\bigr),\qquad F'=\bigl(o',u',(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$$

be two inertial frames of the model with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ and
$(t',x')$, and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be a worldline of a particle label described
in $F$, with coordinate curve $x:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ and coordinate velocity and
acceleration $w=x'$ and $a=x''$ in the sense of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. Then:

1. There are $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$
   ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) such that for every event $p\in A$

$$t'(p)=t(p)+b,\qquad x'(p)=R\,x(p)+v\,t(p)+a_{0}.$$

   The parameters have dimensions $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{0,j}]=\ell$ and
   $[v_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$, and $R$ is dimensionless
   ([[def-cm01-units]]); they are the ones that occur in the adopted class of
   frame changes of [[post-cm01-frames]].

2. Let $\eta:I+b\to\mathbb R^{3}$ be the coordinate curve of the same label in
   $F'$, defined by $\eta(t'):=x'(\gamma(t'-b))$ for $t'\in I+b$. Then $\eta$
   is of class $C^{2}$ and

$$\eta'(t')=R\,w(t'-b)+v,\qquad \eta''(t')=R\,a(t'-b)\qquad(t'\in I+b).$$

3. The coordinate acceleration vanishes identically in one frame exactly when
   it does in the other:

$$a\equiv0\ \text{on}\ I\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \eta''\equiv0\ \text{on}\ I+b.$$

   Equivalently, the property "the coordinate curve is an affine function of
   the frame time" is an inertial-frame-independent property of the motion.

4. Write $G(b,a_{0},v,R)$ for the transformation
   $(t,x)\mapsto(t+b,\,Rx+v\,t+a_{0})$ of the coordinate space. Then

$$G(b_{2},a_{2},v_{2},R_{2})\circ G(b_{1},a_{1},v_{1},R_{1})=G\bigl(b_{1}+b_{2},\ R_{2}a_{1}+v_{2}b_{1}+a_{2},\ R_{2}v_{1}+v_{2},\ R_{2}R_{1}\bigr)$$

and

$$G(b,a_{0},v,R)^{-1}=G\bigl(-b,\ -R^{\mathsf T}(a_{0}-vb),\ -R^{\mathsf T}v,\ R^{\mathsf T}\bigr),$$

   with all parameters again in $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R^{3}\times SO(3)$. Consequently the Galilean transformations form a group of transformations of the coordinate space, and the relation on inertial frames "the two charts differ by a Galilean transformation" is an equivalence relation.

Let an inertial frame $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ be fixed, and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be the worldline of a
particle label described in this frame as in [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; thus
$\gamma$ is of class $C^{2}$, parametrized so that $t(\gamma(s))=s$ for all
$s\in I$, and

$$\gamma(s)=o+su+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\xi_{j}(s)\,e_{j}$$

for the unique coordinate functions $\xi_{j}:I\to\mathbb R$ of the point
$\gamma(s)$ in the adapted chart ([[def-cm-affine-time-space]],
[[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]]).

**(a) The coordinate curve.** The **coordinate curve** of $\gamma$ in the
frame is

$$x_{\gamma}:=\bigl(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3}\bigr):I\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3}.$$

It is of class $C^{2}$ by the regularity clause of [[post-cm01-worldlines]],
and it determines $\gamma$ by the display above, since the parameter condition
fixes the time coordinate. It has dimension $[\,\xi_{j}\,]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(b) Coordinate velocity and acceleration.** The **derivative** of a
vector-valued map is taken componentwise: for the map $x_{\gamma}$ above, its
derivative at $s$ is

$$x_{\gamma}'(s):=\bigl(\xi_{1}'(s),\xi_{2}'(s),\xi_{3}'(s)\bigr),$$

where each $\xi_{j}'(s)=\lim_{h\to0}\bigl(\xi_{j}(s+h)-\xi_{j}(s)\bigr)/h$ is
the ordinary derivative of a real function. The **coordinate velocity** of the
label in the frame is

$$w(s):=x_{\gamma}'(s)\in\mathbb R^{3},$$

with components $w_{j}=\xi_{j}'$, and the **coordinate acceleration** is the
coordinate velocity of the velocity,

$$a(s):=w'(s)=x_{\gamma}''(s)\in\mathbb R^{3}.$$

Their dimensions are $[w_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[a_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-2}$, read
in metres per second and metres per second squared. The triple $w(s)$ is the
triple of numbers read in the frame's axes: it is a coordinate description,
not an element of spacetime.

**(c) Spatial velocity and acceleration vectors.** For the affine curve
$\gamma:I\to A$, subtraction of events uses the affine displacement in $V$.
Define its derivative by the limit in the finite-dimensional vector space
$V$,
$$\gamma'(s):=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\gamma(s+h)-\gamma(s)}{h}=u+\sum_j\xi_j'(s)e_j,$$
and define $\gamma''(s)$ as the derivative of the $V$-valued map
$\gamma'$. This is the canonical identification of each affine tangent
space with $V$; the $C^2$ coordinate regularity guarantees both limits.
The frame's time direction
$u$ and spatial basis identify two elements of the spatial displacement space
$K$ attached to the motion:

$$\underline{v}(s):=\gamma'(s)-u=\sum_{j=1}^{3}w_{j}(s)\,e_{j}\in K,\qquad \underline{a}(s):=\gamma''(s)=\sum_{j=1}^{3}a_{j}(s)\,e_{j}\in K.$$

Here $\gamma'(s)-u$ indeed lies in $K=\ker\tau$, because $\tau(\gamma'(s))=\frac{d}{ds}\tau(\gamma(s)-o)=1$ by linearity of $\tau$ and the parameter condition. The vectors $\underline{v}(s)$ and $\underline{a}(s)$ are the **spatial velocity vector** and **spatial acceleration vector** of the label in the frame; the velocity depends on the frame time direction $u$, whereas the acceleration is an intrinsic element of $K$ unchanged by an inertial frame change (time shifts have derivative $1$). Their coordinates in the frame's basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ are the triples $w(s)$ and $a(s)$.

**(d) Speed.** The **speed** of the label in the frame at time $s$ is the
Euclidean norm $\|w(s)\|_{2}=\sqrt{\sum_{j}w_{j}(s)^{2}}$, of dimension
$\ell\tau^{-1}$; equivalently $\|\underline{v}(s)\|_{2}=\sqrt{g(\underline{v}(s),\underline{v}(s))}$,
the norm induced by the spatial metric, since the basis is $g$-orthonormal.

**(e) Transformation under a change of inertial frame (recorded).** Let a
second inertial frame be given, with coordinates $(t',x')$ and transformation
parameters $(b,a,v,R)$ as in [[post-cm01-frames]], and let
$\eta(t'):=x'(\gamma(t'-b))\in\mathbb R^{3}$ be the description of the motion
in the second frame. Then

$$\eta'(t')=R\,w(t'-b)+v,\qquad \eta''(t')=R\,a(t'-b),$$

that is, in the differentiated variables and abbreviated notation
$w'=Rw+v$ and $a'=Ra$. This law is clause 2 of the mathematical transformation
law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], recorded here
in the model's notation; the definition itself asserts neither law. The
model-level statement of the law, including the frame-independence of the
property $a\equiv0$, is proved as a theorem later on this page.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

derivations.claim: The data of the Example satisfy [L1]: $\tau$ is linear and surjective (its value is the first coordinate), $K=\{0\}\times\mathbb R^{3}$ has dimension three, the standard inner product on $K$ is symmetric and positive definite, the standard orientation of $\mathbb R^{3}$ orients $K$, and $A=\mathbb R^{4}$ is an affine space over itself.

The constructed frame $F'$ is inertial in the sense of [L2]: $\tau(u')=1$ because $u'=(1,-\frac12,0,0)$, and the basis $(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')=(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is $g$-orthonormal and positively oriented; hence $F'$ is an adapted chart with adapted coordinates $(t',x')$.

The primed coordinates of the event $p=tu+\sum_{j}x^{j}e_{j}$ are obtained by expanding $p=o'+t'u'+\sum_{j}x'^{j}e_{j}'$: comparing components gives $t'=t+2$ and $x'=\bigl(x^{1}+\frac12t,\ x^{2}+3,\ x^{3}\bigr)=Rx+vt+a$, so the two frames differ by the transformation of [L3] with the displayed parameters $(b,a,v,R)$.

The prescribed worldline $\gamma$ is of class $C^{\infty}$ and its $F$-time coordinate is $\tau(\gamma(s)-o)=s$, so the parameter condition holds; its coordinate curve is $x(s)$ with coordinate velocity $w=(\frac14,0,0)$ and coordinate acceleration $\alpha(s):=x''(s)=0$.

The primed description of the motion is $\eta(t')=x(t'-2)+v(t'-2)+a=\bigl(\frac34t'-\frac12,\ 5,\ 0\bigr)$; hence $\eta'=(\frac34,0,0)=Rw+v$ and $\eta''(t')=(0,0,0)=R\alpha(t'-b)$, so the velocity and acceleration laws of [L3] hold on this motion, and the vanishing of the coordinate acceleration is frame-independent for it.
As a cross-check, at $t=2$ the $F$-coordinates are $(\frac32,2,0)$ and the $F'$-coordinates of the same event are $\eta(4)=(\frac52,5,0)$, which equals $x(2)+2v+a$ by the transformation of step 1.3.

Finally, the spatial velocity vectors confirm the same laws: in $F$ one has $\underline{v}=\gamma'(s)-u=\frac14e_{1}$, and in $F'$ one has $\underline{v}'=\gamma'(s)-u'=\frac14e_{1}+\frac12e_{1}=\frac34e_{1}$, whose primed-basis coordinates $(\frac34,0,0)$ equal the coordinate velocity $\eta'$ of step 2.1; the example thus verifies the transformation law and the velocity and acceleration laws on explicit data. It does not identify the displayed uniform motion with the motion of an unforced particle in any dynamical sense, which requires the force postulates of a later page.

boundaries.reason: The example uses one explicit event set, one worldline and one interval; no empty family or empty index set occurs and no existence claim about an empty case is made.

boundaries.evidence: The zero entries of the data are checked explicitly: $\tau$ vanishes on $K$, the boost acts trivially on $x^{2},x^{3}$, and step 1.4 computes the constant-velocity motion with $w=(\frac14,0,0)$ and $a=0$.
The example is a single-frame-pair, single-worldline computation: step 1.2 verifies the one constructed frame $F'$, and steps 2.1-4.1 verify the laws on the one motion.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate limit (zero boost, zero rotation) is taken in the computation; the parameters $v=(\frac12,0,0)$, $R=I_{3}$ are fixed and nonzero where displayed, and the general degenerate cases are covered by the theorem, not claimed here.
The motion is defined on all of $\mathbb R$ and the frame change is affine on the whole event space; no endpoint or boundary point is evaluated.
Every quantity of the example is computed from the fixed data; no selection from a family is made and no choice principle is used.
The example verifies the transformation and its velocity and acceleration laws; it asserts no equivalence statement whose forward direction would need a case.
For the same reason the example asserts no converse equivalence.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the set of $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb R$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), with identity $I_3$ and product as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], transpose $R^{\mathsf T}$ as in [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and determinant $\det R$ as in [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].

The **orthogonal group** and the **special orthogonal group** are the subsets

$$O(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\},\qquad SO(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\ \text{and}\ \det R=1\}.$$

Equivalently $SO(3)=O(3)\cap\{R:\det R=1\}$. Elements of $SO(3)$ are called **rotations**. The identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with the function space $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ is the one of [[def-matrix-space]]; when $M_3(\mathbb R)$ is regarded as a metric or topological space, this is always the Euclidean metric of that identification.

In the notation of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]:

1. $I_3\in SO(3)$, and for all $R,S\in SO(3)$ the matrices $RS$ and $R^{\mathsf T}$ again lie in $SO(3)$; moreover $\det R=1$, $R$ is invertible, and its inverse is $R^{\mathsf T}$, so also $RR^{\mathsf T}=I_3$.
2. Consequently $SO(3)$ is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]], [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]).

Use one-based labels $z_i:=z(i-1)$ and $A_{ij}:=A(i-1,j-1)$ for $1\le i,j\le3$, so the displayed components correspond in order to the imported coordinates $0,1,2$. Matrix-vector products mean $(Az)(k):=\sum_{j<3}A(k,j)z(j)$, obtained from the rectangular product by representing $z$ as the column $C_z(j,0)=z(j)$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]).

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval, let $R:I\to SO(3)$ and $c:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be twice continuously differentiable in the sense that all entries of $R$ and all components of $c$ have continuous second derivatives, and put

$$\Omega(t):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)\qquad(t\in I).$$

1. $\Omega(t)$ is skew-symmetric for every $t\in I$, that is $\Omega(t)^{\mathsf T}=-\Omega(t)$.
2. For every $t\in I$ there is exactly one vector $\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3$ such that

$$\Omega(t)z=\omega(t)\times z\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^3),$$

$$SO(3)=\left\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3},\ \det R=1\right\}$$

in the sense of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A rotation acts on spatial
column vectors by matrix multiplication; its entries are dimensionless under
the radian convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Rotations are part of the
formulation of spatial changes of basis; the definition of $SO(3)$ itself
asserts nothing about physical space.

**(ii) Inertial frames.** An **inertial frame** is the global adapted affine
chart of the spacetime data determined by

$$o\in A,\qquad u\in V\ \text{with}\ \tau(u)=1,\qquad (e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\ \text{an ordered,}\ g\text{-orthonormal, positively oriented basis of }K,$$

coordinate is $t(p)=\tau(p-o)$ and the spatial coordinates are the coefficients
of $p-o-tu\in K$ in the basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$. Existence and uniqueness
of the coordinates, and the affine structure of the slices, are the mathematical
content of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]] and
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]]; no physical claim beyond the reading of clause
(iii) is attached to them here.

An inertial frame is a **coordinate chart**: the triple $(o,u,(e_{i}))$. It is
definitively not an observer congruence and not a time-varying basis field. In
the model the basis $(e_{i})$ is fixed once and for all; a family of bases
depending on the time coordinate is a different structure, whose kinematics is
defined separately where it is used, and is not an inertial frame. The physical
reading of the frame is that $t$ is the model's time coordinate in seconds and
$x$ the spatial position in metres, by the conventions of
[[def-cm01-units]].

$\alpha_{x_{0}}:\mathbb R\to A$, $\alpha_{x_{0}}(t):=o+tu+\sum_{j=1}^{3}(x_{0})_{j}e_{j}$,

$\{\alpha_{x_{0}}\}_{x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}}$ is the **stationary observer
congruence** of the frame. Each curve has $t(\alpha_{x_{0}}(s))=s$, is
$C^{\infty}$ in adapted coordinates, and in the frame's own spatial
coordinates has constant coordinate triple $x_{0}$. Here an **observer
worldline** means precisely a $C^2$ curve $\alpha:I\to A$ on a nondegenerate
open real interval with $t(\alpha(s))=s$, used to describe an observer; the
stationary curves just defined have $I=\mathbb R$. This kinematic definition
assigns neither a particle label nor a mass or a dynamical law to an observer.

particle postulate. The congruence is a derived object, determined by the frame and the spacetime data, not an additional primitive. Distinct frames can have the same family of parametrized curves: if $o' = o+\sum_jc_je_j$ while $u'=u$ and $e_j'=e_j$, then $\alpha'_{x_0}(t)=\alpha_{x_0+c}(t)$ for all $t$. transformations between inertial frames

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x'=Rx+vt+a,$$

where $b\in\mathbb R$ is a **time shift** ($[b]=\tau$), $a\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a
**spatial translation** ($[a_{i}]=\ell$), $v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a **boost
velocity** ($[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$) and $R\in SO(3)$ a **rotation**
($[R_{ij}]=1$). Every pair of inertial frames is related by exactly one such
transformation: that two adapted charts of the same data differ by a
transformation of this form, with $R\in SO(3)$ because both bases are
positively oriented, is the mathematical transformation law proved in
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]. acceleration, and the frame-independence of zero coordinate acceleration — are
proved as a statement about the model in
[[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

those pages adopt, as the content of Newton's first law, that there exist
inertial frames in the sense of clause (ii) in which a particle with zero
applied interaction has zero coordinate acceleration. This postulate
introduces the frames and their changes but asserts no dynamics: it does not
state that any particular motion has zero acceleration, and it does not
privilege any one inertial frame — each of them is a legitimate arena for the
formulation of the model's equations.

coordinate changes. A quantity is **conserved along a motion** when its value as a function of the frame time is constant on the interval of that motion. No such constancy is asserted here, nor is it asserted that every
mechanical system's description is invariant in form; a force law must also
transform appropriately under (iv) to be a law of the model in every frame, and

description of a concrete experiment. Conservation statements, when they hold,
are theorems of later pages with their own hypotheses, not consequences of
this postulate.

$s\in I$, and

$\gamma(s)$ in the adapted chart ([[def-cm-affine-time-space]],

fixes the time coordinate. It has dimension $[\,\xi_{j}\,]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]).

model-level statement of the law, including the frame-independence of the
property $a\equiv0$, is proved as a theorem later on this page.

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

The worldline $\gamma$ with $F$-coordinate curve $x(s)=(1,0,0)$ is a worldline of the model: it is of class $C^{\infty}$ and satisfies the parameter condition, and its coordinate velocity and acceleration in $F$ are $w=0$ and $a=0$; its spatial velocity vector in $F$ is $\underline v=\gamma'(s)-u=0$.

Hence $R(s)\in SO(3)$ for every $s$: the columns of $R(s)$ are the coordinates of $(\tilde e_{1}(s),\tilde e_{2}(s),\tilde e_{3}(s))$ and form a positively oriented orthonormal basis, so $R(s)^{\mathsf T}R(s)=I_{3}$ and $\det R(s)=1$ by [L3]; moreover $\sin$ and $\cos$ are continuous because differentiable. Inductively, if both are $C^k$, their derivatives $\cos$ and $-\sin$ are $C^k$ by [L1], so both are $C^{k+1}$. Thus they are $C^{\infty}$; composing with $s\mapsto\omega s$ by [L7] gives $C^{\infty}$ entries of $R$ and $R^{\mathsf T}$.

The rotating-basis coordinate curve is $y(s)=R(s)^{\mathsf T}x(s)=\bigl(\cos(\omega s),\,-\sin(\omega s),\,0\bigr)$, because $R(s)^{\mathsf T}$ has first column $(\cos(\omega s),-\sin(\omega s),0)$; differentiating with the chain rule [L7] and step 2.1 gives $y'(s)=\omega\bigl(-\sin(\omega s),\,-\cos(\omega s),\,0\bigr)$ and $y''(s)=-\omega^{2}\bigl(\cos(\omega s),\,-\sin(\omega s),\,0\bigr)=-\omega^{2}y(s)$, so $y''\not\equiv0$ because $y$ is never the zero vector (its norm is $1$ by [L2]).

The identity of [L4] applies with $c=0$, $x''=0$ and, from $\Omega=R^{\mathsf T}R'$ computed from the displayed $R$, with $\boldsymbol\omega$ the constant vector $(0,0,\omega)$; by steps 2.1 and 3.1 the two sides read $R^{\mathsf T}x''=0$ and $y''+2\boldsymbol\omega\times y'+\boldsymbol\omega'\times y+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times y)=0$, since $2\boldsymbol\omega\times y'=2\omega^{2}y$, $\boldsymbol\omega'\times y=0$ and $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times y)=-\omega^{2}y$, so the displayed identity is satisfied on this example. Every term has acceleration dimension $\ell\tau^{-2}$; the scalar $\omega$ retains the inverse-time dimension declared in the Example.

The result $y''\not\equiv0$ of step 3.1, together with $x''\equiv0$ in the inertial frame $F$, shows that the rotating basis is **not** an inertial frame of the model: were it inertial, its coordinate acceleration of the same worldline would have to vanish identically by clause 3 of [L5], contradicting step 3.1; equivalently, an inertial frame of the model has a constant spatial basis by [L5], and the basis field $\tilde e_{j}(s)$ is not constant. The example therefore delimits the frame assumptions: a time-dependent change of basis preserves simultaneity and the time coordinate but does not preserve the uniform-motion property, and the two extra terms displayed in step 4.1 are kinematic coordinate effects in this basis, not a force law.

$w'=Rw+v$ and $a'=Ra$. This law is clause 2 of the mathematical transformation
law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], recorded here
in the model's notation; the definition itself asserts neither law. The
model-level statement of the law, including the frame-independence of the
property $a\equiv0$, is proved as a theorem later on this page.

Take the concrete model data

$$V=\mathbb R^{4},\qquad \tau(x^{0},x^{1},x^{2},x^{3})=x^{0},\qquad K=\{0\}\times\mathbb R^{3},$$

with $g$ the standard Euclidean inner product $g\bigl((0,u),(0,w)\bigr)=u\cdot w$ on $K$, the standard orientation of $K$, and $A=\mathbb R^{4}$ with its standard affine structure over $V$; the coordinates are read with $t$ in seconds and $(x^{1},x^{2},x^{3})$ in metres. Adopt the spacetime, frame and worldline postulates
([[post-cm01-spacetime]], [[post-cm01-frames]], [[post-cm01-worldlines]]).

**First frame.** $F=(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ with $o=0$,
$u=(1,0,0,0)$, $e_{1}=(0,1,0,0)$, $e_{2}=(0,0,1,0)$, $e_{3}=(0,0,0,1)$.
The adapted coordinates are the standard ones, written
$(t,x)=(t,x^{1},x^{2},x^{3})$.

**Transformation data.** Choose

$$b=2\,\mathrm s,\qquad a=(0,\,3\,\mathrm m,\,0),\qquad v=\Bigl(\frac12,\,0,\,0\Bigr)\ \mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1},\qquad R=I_{3}.$$

**Second frame constructed from the data.** Put
$e_{j}'=e_{j}$ for $j=1,2,3$ (the rotation is trivial),
$u'=u-\sum_{j}v_{j}e_{j}'=(1,-\frac12,0,0)$ and
$o'=o-bu-\sum_{j}\bigl(R^{\mathsf T}(a-vb)\bigr)_{j}e_{j}=(-2,\,1,\,-3,\,0)$;
write $(t',x')$ for the adapted coordinates of
$F'=(o',u',(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}'))$.

**The motion.** Let $\gamma:\mathbb R\to A$ be the worldline whose
$F$-coordinates are

$$\gamma(s)=\bigl(s,\ 1+\tfrac14 s,\ 2,\ 0\bigr),$$

that is, the coordinate curve $x(s)=\bigl(1+\tfrac14 s,\ 2,\ 0\bigr)$ with
constant coordinate velocity
$w=(\tfrac14,0,0)\ \mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$ and zero coordinate
acceleration.

derivations.claim: In the frame $F$ the worldline has coordinate velocity $w=x'=(\frac14,0,0)$: differentiating $x(s)=(1+\frac14s,\,2,\,0)$ gives $w=(\frac14,0,0)$, independent of $s$.

In the frame $F'$ the primed coordinate curve of the same worldline is $\eta(t')=(\frac34t'-\frac12,\,5,\,0)$, whose derivative is $\eta'(t')=(\frac34,0,0)$; this agrees with the velocity law $\eta'=Rw+v=(\frac14,0,0)+(\frac12,0,0)=(\frac34,0,0)$ of [L1].

The two coordinate velocities $\eta'=(\frac34,0,0)$ and $w=(\frac14,0,0)$ differ: their first components $\frac34\ne\frac14$. The refuted statement therefore fails for this worldline and this pair of inertial frames; the correct law is $w'=Rw+v$ of clause 2 of [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]], which is what step 2.1 verified, and the coordinate acceleration $a=0$ is preserved, in accordance with clause 3 of the same theorem.

boundaries.evidence: The zero case is the sharp one: a particle with zero coordinate velocity in $F$ has nonzero coordinate velocity in $F'$, which step 3.1 states as the limiting case $w=0$.

No degenerate limit is taken: the boost velocity $v=(\frac12,0,0)$ is nonzero and the rotation is trivial; the general case is covered by the theorem.

The quantities are computed from fixed data with no selection and no choice principle.

Let $N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ be given as
in [[post-cm01-worldlines]], and fix one inertial frame of the model with
spatial coordinates $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ for each label $i$. Identify the
space of all position tuples with $\mathbb R^{3N}=(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and
write its points as $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$; each component $x_{i}$ has
dimension $\ell$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an
open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple
$x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to
each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the
**collision set**

$$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$

from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at
coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many
closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map
$x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a
legitimate configuration domain. Whether the exclusion is part of the model is
a modelling decision recorded with the force law; the framework itself only
requires $Q$ to be open and stated.

**(b) Holonomic constraint branch.** Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ be an open
**ambient set**, let $k\in\mathbb N$ with $1\le k\le3N-1$, and let

$$G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{k}):O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k}$$

be a smooth map, each component carrying a declared dimension and unit fixed
by the model (a component can always be rescaled by a nonzero constant without
changing its zero set, and the rescaling is part of the declaration). Assume:

1. **Nonempty level set:** $G^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing$;
2. **Rank condition:** the differential $DG(x):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k}$
   is surjective, equivalently has rank $k$, at every $x\in G^{-1}(0)$.

Then $0$ is a regular value of $G$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]], and the **constrained
configuration space** is $Q:=G^{-1}(0)$. By
[[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] — applied to the smooth
map $G$ from the open subset $O$ of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ to $\mathbb R^{k}$, whose
regular value $0$ has nonempty fibre — $Q$ is an embedded submanifold of
$\mathbb R^{3N}$ of dimension $3N-k$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]).
The **degrees of freedom** of this branch of the model is the number
$$\dim Q=3N-k.$$ In the sense of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]], $Q$ together with the inclusion $X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ is then a particle configuration, and the mass metric of that definition is available with the masses $m_{i}$; the configuration is constrained to $Q$ for all times in this branch.

**(c) Time-dependent holonomic constraints.** If the constraint map depends on
time,

$$G:\mathbb R\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k},\qquad (t,x)\longmapsto G(t,x),$$

with $G$ smooth and $D_{x}G(t_{0},x)$ of rank $k$ at every $x$ of the nonempty
set $G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$, then for each fixed $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$ the
**instantaneous configuration space** $Q_{t_{0}}:=G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$ is an
embedded submanifold of dimension $3N-k$ by the same theorem applied to
$G(t_{0},\cdot)$. The family $\{Q_{t_{0}}\}$ varies with $t_{0}$; a curve
$t\mapsto q(t)$ with $G(t,q(t))=0$ is not thereby a curve in one fixed
manifold, and the kinematic treatment of such constraints (velocities, the
reaction forces that maintain them and the distinction between rheonomic and
scleronomic constraints) belongs to the framework's constraint development and
is not part of this definition.

**(d) Mass operator.** In the ambient coordinates define the **mass operator**
$\mathsf M:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ by block multiplication,

$$\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N});$$

its matrix in the standard basis is block diagonal with blocks $m_{i}I_{3}$,
the **mass matrix** of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]].
Its dimension is $\mu$: it multiplies positions of dimension $\ell$ by masses
of dimension $\mu$. On the constrained branch, for the inclusion
$X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ and tangent vectors $h,z\in T_qQ$,
the mass metric of that item is
$$\mathcal G_q(h,z):=\langle dX_q(h),\mathsf M\,dX_q(z)\rangle_{3N}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_i\,h_i\cdot z_i,$$
where $h_i,z_i\in\mathbb R^3$ are the blocks of $dX_q(h),dX_q(z)$ under
the canonical Euclidean tangent identification specified in that supplier.
It restricts the mass-weighted ambient bilinear form to $T_qQ$, rather than
the unweighted Euclidean inner product.

**(e) Velocity constraints are a different object.** A **velocity-map
constraint** on the open ambient set $O$ is a pair of smooth maps
$$A:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'\times3N},\qquad b:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'},\qquad 1\le k'\le3N,$$
with $A(t,x)$ of constant rank $k'$ everywhere in the declared domain,
imposing $A(t,x(t))\dot x(t)+b(t,x(t))=0$ on a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to O$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval, the parameter $t$ is frame time, and $\dot x(t):=x'(t)$ is the componentwise derivative in the convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Equivalently $A(t,x)$ is a linear map
$\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k'}$. Each row's output unit is declared, and
its corresponding component of $b$ has that same unit. The allowed velocities
at $(t,x)$ form the affine set $\{v:A(t,x)v+b(t,x)=0\}$; its differences form
$\ker A(t,x)$.

The law is **locally holonomic-equivalent at $(t_0,x_0)$** if on some open
neighbourhood $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times O$ of that point there are a $C^2$
map $g:V\to\mathbb R^{k'}$ with $D_xg$ of rank $k'$ and a $C^2$ matrix map
$C:V\to\mathbb R^{k'\times k'}$ with $\det C\ne0$ such that
$$A=C\,D_xg,\qquad b=C\,\partial_tg\qquad\text{on }V.$$
Thus the velocity law is locally the derivative of the regular positional
constraints $g(t,x)=\text{constant}$. It is **locally nonholonomic at the
specified point** when no such neighbourhood and pair $(g,C)$ exists; a
nonholonomic model in this local sense declares a point (or a region of
points) with this failure. For a homogeneous time-independent law this
rules out such a regular-level-set representation throughout a neighbourhood.
It need not rule out an individual embedded submanifold $S\subseteq O$ with
$T_xS=\ker A(x)$ for every $x\in S$, using the ambient tangent identification
of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]]; for an affine
time-dependent law the criterion also includes the drift $b$.
Absence of a single global pair alone does not establish local
nonintegrability. The rank of $A$ counts instantaneous velocity restrictions,
not the dimension of a positional configuration manifold; accessibility
requires its own definition. Rank changes require a separate model.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth, let $q\in N$ be a regular value, and assume
$F^{-1}(q)$ is nonempty. Then $F^{-1}(q)$ is an embedded submanifold of
codimension $n$. Equivalently, it has dimension $m-n$.

Let $N\ge1$; the ambient dimension is $3N$. Identify $\mathbb R^{3N}$ with the $N$-fold product $(\mathbb R^3)^N$ and write a point as $x=(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ with $x_i\in\mathbb R^3$, explicitly $x_i(k):=x(3(i-1)+k)$ for $1\le i\le N$ and $0\le k<3$; the Euclidean inner product on $\mathbb R^{3N}$ is

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{3N}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_2,$$

with $\langle\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\rangle_2$ the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $d\ge0$ and let $Q$ be a smooth $d$-dimensional manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) and let

$$X:Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$$

be a smooth map. The manifold $Q$ is the **configuration space** and $X$ is the **configuration map**; the pair $(Q,X)$ is called a **particle configuration** when $Q$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ and $X$ is the inclusion ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]), and a **parametrized configuration** otherwise. For $q\in Q$ the intrinsic differential is $dX_q:T_qQ\to T_{X(q)}\mathbb R^{3N}$ as in [[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]] ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]] for the tangent space). For $a\in\mathbb R^{3N}$ and the coordinate function $\pi_k(x):=x(k)$, define $\iota_a:T_a\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ by $\iota_a(w)(k):=w([\pi_k])$ for $0\le k<3N$. This is the standard linear isomorphism: in the identity chart the coordinate derivations form a basis by [[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]], and evaluation on coordinate germs sends that basis to the standard unit vectors. Throughout this item and its mass-metric formulas, the notation $dX_q(u)$ in Euclidean expressions abbreviates $\iota_{X(q)}(dX_q(u))$. In particular its components are $u([\pi_k\circ X])$, so this convention retains the usual Jacobian and inclusion formulas.

Let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ be **masses**. The **mass matrix** is the linear map $M:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ acting on each block by $M(x_1,\dots,x_N)=(m_1x_1,\dots,m_Nx_N)$; its matrix in the standard basis is block diagonal with blocks $m_iI_3$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]).

The **mass metric** of $(Q,X,m_1,\dots,m_N)$ is the family of maps

$$G_q:T_qQ\times T_qQ\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad G_q(u,v):=\langle dX_q(u),\,M\,dX_q(v)\rangle_{3N},$$

for $q\in Q$ and $u,v\in T_qQ$. The **kinetic energy** of a tangent vector $v\in T_qQ$ is

$$T_q(v):=\tfrac12\,G_q(v,v).$$

Each $G_q$ is a symmetric bilinear form on the real vector space $T_qQ$ in the sense of [[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]; that the family depends smoothly on $q$ means that in every smooth local chart of $Q$ the coefficient functions $q\mapsto G_q(\partial_i,\partial_j)$ are smooth, and is stated in the smoothness remark below.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: $\Delta$ is closed, hence $Q_{0}=\mathbb R^{6}\setminus\Delta$ is open: for $x\notin\Delta$ the number $\delta:=\|x_{1}-x_{2}\|_{2}$ is positive, and every $y\in\mathbb R^{6}$ with $\|y-x\|_{2}<\delta/4$ satisfies $\|y_{1}-y_{2}\|_{2}\ge\|x_{1}-x_{2}\|_{2}-\|y_{1}-x_{1}\|_{2}-\|y_{2}-x_{2}\|_{2}>\delta-\delta/4-\delta/4=\delta/2>0$, so $y\notin\Delta$; the ball of radius $\delta/4$ about $x$ therefore lies in $Q_{0}$, and $Q_{0}$ is open as required by [L1].

The differential of $G$: for $x\in\mathbb R^{6}$ and $u=(u_{1},u_{2})\in\mathbb R^{6}$ one has $G(x+su)-G(x)=2s\langle x_{1}-x_{2},u_{1}-u_{2}\rangle_{2}+s^{2}\|u_{1}-u_{2}\|_{2}^{2}$ by bilinearity of the inner product [L4], so $DG(x)(u)=2\langle x_{1}-x_{2},\,u_{1}-u_{2}\rangle_{2}$; this linear functional is nonzero exactly when $x_{1}\ne x_{2}$, since it vanishes for all $u$ only if $x_{1}=x_{2}$, while if $x_{1}\ne x_{2}$ then $u=(x_{1}-x_{2},0)$ gives $DG(x)(u)=2\|x_{1}-x_{2}\|_{2}^{2}>0$; hence $DG(x)$ has rank $1$ exactly on the complement of $\Delta$.

On the zero set the rank condition holds: if $G(x)=0$ then $\|x_{1}-x_{2}\|_{2}^{2}=\ell^{2}>0$, so $x_{1}\ne x_{2}$ and $DG(x)$ is surjective by step 1.2; and $G^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing$, for instance $x_{1}=0$ and $x_{2}=\ell e_{1}$ give $G(x)=\ell^{2}-\ell^{2}=0$; thus $0$ is a regular value of $G$ with nonempty level set.

By the regular level set theorem [L2], applied to the smooth map $G:\mathbb R^{6}\to\mathbb R$ with the regular value $0$, the set $Q=G^{-1}(0)$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb R^{6}$ of dimension $6-1=5$; by [L1] the rigid-rod branch therefore has $5=3\cdot2-1$ configuration degrees of freedom, in agreement with the identification of the same constraint in the cited treatment. With the masses $m_{1},m_{2}$, the pair consisting of $Q$ and the inclusion is a particle configuration whose mass matrix is $M=\operatorname{diag}(m_{1}I_{3},m_{2}I_{3})$ and whose mass metric is that of [L3]; the constraint function $G$ has dimension $\ell^{2}$, and rescaling it by any nonzero constant leaves both its zero set and the rank condition on that set unchanged, as recorded in [L1].

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 verifies the nonemptiness hypothesis explicitly by exhibiting $x_{1}=0$, $x_{2}=\ell e_{1}$ with $G(x)=0$, which the regular level set theorem requires.
The zero cases of the constraints are treated: the excluded collision set is exactly the zero set of $x_{1}-x_{2}$, and the rank of $DG$ is computed at the zero level $G=0$ in steps 1.2-2.1.
The example is the $N=2$, $k=1$ case, and the computation is carried out for that single constraint component: step 3.1 specialises $3N-k=6-1=5$.

boundaries.reason: The degenerate value $\ell=0$ is excluded by the hypothesis $\ell>0$; for $\ell=0$ the level set would be the diagonal, not a regular level, and the statement does not claim it.
The configuration domain is an open set or a level manifold without boundary; no interval endpoints are evaluated.
The proof uses no selection; the witness pair of step 2.1 is written explicitly.
The example asserts no equivalence; it verifies the hypotheses and conclusion of the regular level set theorem in one case.
The Example specifies the positive-length two-particle rod and verifies its configuration locus and Jacobian rank; no equivalence of two propositions is asserted by this worked configuration.

risk_review.notes: Checked steps 1.1-3.1 with N=2, positive masses and h=ell>0: norm-ball radius delta/4 excludes the diagonal, polynomial G is smooth, DG(u)=2<x1-x2,u1-u2> is surjective on G=0, and (0,ell e1) witnesses nonemptiness. Exact regular-level theorem requires a smooth map and nonempty regular fibre and gives 6-1=5. Ell=0 is excluded and would fail rank. The block mass map and inclusion agree with the current supplier whose ambient dimension is 3N and whose intrinsic dimension is independently d.
