Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about frames, in the spacetime structure of [[post-cm01-spacetime]].

**(i) Rotations.** A **rotation** is a matrix $R\in SO(3)$, where

$$SO(3)=\left\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3},\ \det R=1\right\}$$

in the sense of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A rotation acts on spatial
column vectors by matrix multiplication; its entries are dimensionless under
the radian convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Rotations are part of the
formulation of spatial changes of basis; the definition of $SO(3)$ itself
asserts nothing about physical space.

**(ii) Inertial frames.** An **inertial frame** is the global adapted affine
chart of the spacetime data determined by

$$o\in A,\qquad u\in V\ \text{with}\ \tau(u)=1,\qquad (e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\ \text{an ordered,}\ g\text{-orthonormal, positively oriented basis of }K,$$

with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ as in [[def-cm-affine-time-space]]: the time
coordinate is $t(p)=\tau(p-o)$ and the spatial coordinates are the coefficients
of $p-o-tu\in K$ in the basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$. Existence and uniqueness
of the coordinates, and the affine structure of the slices, are the mathematical
content of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]] and
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]]; no physical claim beyond the reading of clause
(iii) is attached to them here.

An inertial frame is a **coordinate chart**: the triple $(o,u,(e_{i}))$. It is
definitively not an observer congruence and not a time-varying basis field. In
the model the basis $(e_{i})$ is fixed once and for all; a family of bases
depending on the time coordinate is a different structure, whose kinematics is
defined separately where it is used, and is not an inertial frame. The physical
reading of the frame is that $t$ is the model's time coordinate in seconds and
$x$ the spatial position in metres, by the conventions of
[[def-cm01-units]].

**(iii) Stationary observers.** For $x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ the curve
$\alpha_{x_{0}}:\mathbb R\to A$, $\alpha_{x_{0}}(t):=o+tu+\sum_{j=1}^{3}(x_{0})_{j}e_{j}$,
is the **observer at rest in the frame at position $x_{0}$**; the family
$\{\alpha_{x_{0}}\}_{x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}}$ is the **stationary observer
congruence** of the frame. Each curve has $t(\alpha_{x_{0}}(s))=s$, is
$C^{\infty}$ in adapted coordinates, and in the frame's own spatial
coordinates has constant coordinate triple $x_{0}$. Here an **observer
worldline** means precisely a $C^2$ curve $\alpha:I\to A$ on a nondegenerate
open real interval with $t(\alpha(s))=s$, used to describe an observer; the
stationary curves just defined have $I=\mathbb R$. This kinematic definition
assigns neither a particle label nor a mass or a dynamical law to an observer.
A particle worldline will separately be assigned to a particle label in the
particle postulate. The congruence is a derived object, determined by the frame and the spacetime data, not an additional primitive. Distinct frames can have the same family of parametrized curves: if $o' = o+\sum_jc_je_j$ while $u'=u$ and $e_j'=e_j$, then $\alpha'_{x_0}(t)=\alpha_{x_0+c}(t)$ for all $t$. Thus shifting only the spatial origin relabels this family. Changing $u$ changes the curve family, since every curve in it has the affine derivative $u$.

**(iv) Allowed changes between frames.** The model adopts the class of
transformations between inertial frames

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x'=Rx+vt+a,$$

where $b\in\mathbb R$ is a **time shift** ($[b]=\tau$), $a\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a
**spatial translation** ($[a_{i}]=\ell$), $v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a **boost
velocity** ($[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$) and $R\in SO(3)$ a **rotation**
($[R_{ij}]=1$). Every pair of inertial frames is related by exactly one such
transformation: that two adapted charts of the same data differ by a
transformation of this form, with $R\in SO(3)$ because both bases are
positively oriented, is the mathematical transformation law proved in
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]. Uniqueness follows by comparing the coordinate maps on all $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$: evaluating the time map fixes $b$; evaluating the spatial map at $(0,0)$ fixes $a$, at $(1,0)$ fixes $v$, and at $(0,e_j)$ for the three standard coordinate vectors fixes each column of $R$. The kinematic
consequences of the law — the transformation of coordinate velocity and
acceleration, and the frame-independence of zero coordinate acceleration — are
proved as a statement about the model in
[[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(v) Free motion is not asserted here.** The framework's dynamics enters
through the force and equation-of-motion postulates of the pages that follow;
those pages adopt, as the content of Newton's first law, that there exist
inertial frames in the sense of clause (ii) in which a particle with zero
applied interaction has zero coordinate acceleration. This postulate
introduces the frames and their changes but asserts no dynamics: it does not
state that any particular motion has zero acceleration, and it does not
privilege any one inertial frame — each of them is a legitimate arena for the
formulation of the model's equations.

**(vi) Kinematic symmetry is not conservation.** The class (iv) is a class of
coordinate changes. A quantity is **conserved along a motion** when its value as a function of the frame time is constant on the interval of that motion. No such constancy is asserted here, nor is it asserted that every
mechanical system's description is invariant in form; a force law must also
transform appropriately under (iv) to be a law of the model in every frame, and
an external apparatus or background field can single out frames for the
description of a concrete experiment. Conservation statements, when they hold,
are theorems of later pages with their own hypotheses, not consequences of
this postulate.

Adopt the spacetime assumptions of [[post-cm01-spacetime]], the frame
assumptions of [[post-cm01-frames]] and the worldline assumptions of
[[post-cm01-worldlines]]. Let

$$F=\bigl(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\bigr),\qquad F'=\bigl(o',u',(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$$

be two inertial frames of the model with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ and
$(t',x')$, and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be a worldline of a particle label described
in $F$, with coordinate curve $x:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ and coordinate velocity and
acceleration $w=x'$ and $a=x''$ in the sense of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. Then:

1. There are $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$
   ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) such that for every event $p\in A$

$$t'(p)=t(p)+b,\qquad x'(p)=R\,x(p)+v\,t(p)+a_{0}.$$

   The parameters have dimensions $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{0,j}]=\ell$ and
   $[v_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$, and $R$ is dimensionless
   ([[def-cm01-units]]); they are the ones that occur in the adopted class of
   frame changes of [[post-cm01-frames]].

2. Let $\eta:I+b\to\mathbb R^{3}$ be the coordinate curve of the same label in
   $F'$, defined by $\eta(t'):=x'(\gamma(t'-b))$ for $t'\in I+b$. Then $\eta$
   is of class $C^{2}$ and

$$\eta'(t')=R\,w(t'-b)+v,\qquad \eta''(t')=R\,a(t'-b)\qquad(t'\in I+b).$$

3. The coordinate acceleration vanishes identically in one frame exactly when
   it does in the other:

$$a\equiv0\ \text{on}\ I\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \eta''\equiv0\ \text{on}\ I+b.$$

   Equivalently, the property "the coordinate curve is an affine function of
   the frame time" is an inertial-frame-independent property of the motion.

4. Write $G(b,a_{0},v,R)$ for the transformation
   $(t,x)\mapsto(t+b,\,Rx+v\,t+a_{0})$ of the coordinate space. Then

$$G(b_{2},a_{2},v_{2},R_{2})\circ G(b_{1},a_{1},v_{1},R_{1})=G\bigl(b_{1}+b_{2},\ R_{2}a_{1}+v_{2}b_{1}+a_{2},\ R_{2}v_{1}+v_{2},\ R_{2}R_{1}\bigr)$$

and

$$G(b,a_{0},v,R)^{-1}=G\bigl(-b,\ -R^{\mathsf T}(a_{0}-vb),\ -R^{\mathsf T}v,\ R^{\mathsf T}\bigr),$$

   with all parameters again in $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R^{3}\times SO(3)$. Consequently the Galilean transformations form a group of transformations of the coordinate space, and the relation on inertial frames "the two charts differ by a Galilean transformation" is an equivalence relation.

Let an inertial frame $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ be fixed, and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be the worldline of a
particle label described in this frame as in [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; thus
$\gamma$ is of class $C^{2}$, parametrized so that $t(\gamma(s))=s$ for all
$s\in I$, and

$$\gamma(s)=o+su+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\xi_{j}(s)\,e_{j}$$

for the unique coordinate functions $\xi_{j}:I\to\mathbb R$ of the point
$\gamma(s)$ in the adapted chart ([[def-cm-affine-time-space]],
[[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]]).

**(a) The coordinate curve.** The **coordinate curve** of $\gamma$ in the
frame is

$$x_{\gamma}:=\bigl(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3}\bigr):I\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3}.$$

It is of class $C^{2}$ by the regularity clause of [[post-cm01-worldlines]],
and it determines $\gamma$ by the display above, since the parameter condition
fixes the time coordinate. It has dimension $[\,\xi_{j}\,]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(b) Coordinate velocity and acceleration.** The **derivative** of a
vector-valued map is taken componentwise: for the map $x_{\gamma}$ above, its
derivative at $s$ is

$$x_{\gamma}'(s):=\bigl(\xi_{1}'(s),\xi_{2}'(s),\xi_{3}'(s)\bigr),$$

where each $\xi_{j}'(s)=\lim_{h\to0}\bigl(\xi_{j}(s+h)-\xi_{j}(s)\bigr)/h$ is
the ordinary derivative of a real function. The **coordinate velocity** of the
label in the frame is

$$w(s):=x_{\gamma}'(s)\in\mathbb R^{3},$$

with components $w_{j}=\xi_{j}'$, and the **coordinate acceleration** is the
coordinate velocity of the velocity,

$$a(s):=w'(s)=x_{\gamma}''(s)\in\mathbb R^{3}.$$

Their dimensions are $[w_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[a_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-2}$, read
in metres per second and metres per second squared. The triple $w(s)$ is the
triple of numbers read in the frame's axes: it is a coordinate description,
not an element of spacetime.

**(c) Spatial velocity and acceleration vectors.** For the affine curve
$\gamma:I\to A$, subtraction of events uses the affine displacement in $V$.
Define its derivative by the limit in the finite-dimensional vector space
$V$,
$$\gamma'(s):=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\gamma(s+h)-\gamma(s)}{h}=u+\sum_j\xi_j'(s)e_j,$$
and define $\gamma''(s)$ as the derivative of the $V$-valued map
$\gamma'$. This is the canonical identification of each affine tangent
space with $V$; the $C^2$ coordinate regularity guarantees both limits.
The frame's time direction
$u$ and spatial basis identify two elements of the spatial displacement space
$K$ attached to the motion:

$$\underline{v}(s):=\gamma'(s)-u=\sum_{j=1}^{3}w_{j}(s)\,e_{j}\in K,\qquad \underline{a}(s):=\gamma''(s)=\sum_{j=1}^{3}a_{j}(s)\,e_{j}\in K.$$

Here $\gamma'(s)-u$ indeed lies in $K=\ker\tau$, because $\tau(\gamma'(s))=\frac{d}{ds}\tau(\gamma(s)-o)=1$ by linearity of $\tau$ and the parameter condition. The vectors $\underline{v}(s)$ and $\underline{a}(s)$ are the **spatial velocity vector** and **spatial acceleration vector** of the label in the frame; the velocity depends on the frame time direction $u$, whereas the acceleration is an intrinsic element of $K$ unchanged by an inertial frame change (time shifts have derivative $1$). Their coordinates in the frame's basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ are the triples $w(s)$ and $a(s)$.

**(d) Speed.** The **speed** of the label in the frame at time $s$ is the
Euclidean norm $\|w(s)\|_{2}=\sqrt{\sum_{j}w_{j}(s)^{2}}$, of dimension
$\ell\tau^{-1}$; equivalently $\|\underline{v}(s)\|_{2}=\sqrt{g(\underline{v}(s),\underline{v}(s))}$,
the norm induced by the spatial metric, since the basis is $g$-orthonormal.

**(e) Transformation under a change of inertial frame (recorded).** Let a
second inertial frame be given, with coordinates $(t',x')$ and transformation
parameters $(b,a,v,R)$ as in [[post-cm01-frames]], and let
$\eta(t'):=x'(\gamma(t'-b))\in\mathbb R^{3}$ be the description of the motion
in the second frame. Then

$$\eta'(t')=R\,w(t'-b)+v,\qquad \eta''(t')=R\,a(t'-b),$$

that is, in the differentiated variables and abbreviated notation
$w'=Rw+v$ and $a'=Ra$. This law is clause 2 of the mathematical transformation
law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], recorded here
in the model's notation; the definition itself asserts neither law. The
model-level statement of the law, including the frame-independence of the
property $a\equiv0$, is proved as a theorem later on this page.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about particles and their motion, in the spacetime of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and the frames of [[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Particle labels and worldlines.** A model of the framework has **particle
labels** $i=1,\dots,N$ for some $N\ge1$. To each label and each *inertial
frame* of the model — an adapted chart $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ with
coordinates $(t,x)$ in the sense of [[post-cm01-frames]] — there is assigned a
**worldline** $\gamma_{i}:I\to A$ described in that frame, where
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval — that is, an interval
of the form $(a,b)$ with $-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points —
the curve $\gamma_{i}$ is of class $C^{2}$ in the adapted coordinates of the frame,
and the **parameter condition**

$$\tau\bigl(\gamma_{i}(t)-o\bigr)=t\qquad(t\in I)$$

holds: the curve parameter is the elapsed time from the origin of the frame, so
in the frame's coordinates $\gamma_{i}(t)=(t,x_{i}(t))$ with
$x_{i}:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$. The parameter condition replaces
the causal conditions of relativistic kinematics: no timelike condition on the
velocity and no upper bound on its Euclidean norm is imposed, and the
parameter is not free up to reparametrization.

**(ii) Description in another frame.** The same motion described in a second
inertial frame is the curve obtained by the time reparametrization of the two
frames: if $(t',x')$ are the coordinates of the second frame and
$t'=t+b$ is the time component of the transformation between the two frames
([[post-cm01-frames]], [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]),
then the description of the motion in the second frame is the curve
$\gamma_{i,b}(t'):=\gamma_{i}(t'-b)$, defined on $I+b$, and it again satisfies
the parameter condition $\tau(\gamma_{i,b}(t')-o')=t'$ with respect to the
second frame's origin $o'$. This is a consistency requirement of the model's
frame language; the accompanying spatial transformation of the coordinate
curve is the affine law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]],
and its kinematic consequences are proved in [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(iii) Regularity is frame-independent.** The class of the worldline is
independent of the frame used to describe it: by the transformation law of
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], the coordinates of the
same event in two inertial frames differ by
$t'=t+b$, $x'=Rx+vt+a$ with constant $b,a,v$ and $R\in SO(3)$, so a coordinate
curve is twice continuously differentiable in one inertial frame exactly when
its reparametrized description is twice continuously differentiable in the
other. The assumptions of this postulate are therefore read in any one inertial
frame without loss.

**(iv) Velocity and acceleration.** In a fixed inertial frame the quantities
$w_{i}:=dx_{i}/dt$ and $a_{i}:=d^{2}x_{i}/dt^{2}$ are the **coordinate
velocity** and **coordinate acceleration** of the label, of dimensions
$\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ by [[def-cm01-units]]; they are defined
precisely, and their transformation under a change of inertial frame is
recorded, in [[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]].

**(v) Fixed inertial mass.** Each particle label $i$ carries a **mass**
$m_{i}>0$, a primitive parameter of the model with dimension $\mu$
([[def-cm01-units]]). The mass is fixed: it is the same positive number at all
times and in all inertial frames of this model; the index $i$ identifies a label within that model and asserts no cross-model identification or equality of mass parameters. It
is not a function of the time coordinate, of the position or of the velocity,
and no variable-mass model is a model of this clause. The mass enters the
dynamics only through its later appearance in the equation of motion; this
postulate attaches no dynamics to it. Distinct labels may carry distinct
masses, and the masses are model data, not measured values.

**(vi) Point-particle idealization.** The model retains of each label only its
position and its fixed mass, together with the label index: size, shape, spin,
deformation, temperature and internal degrees of freedom are omitted, and the
quantity $x_{i}(t)$ is the single point representing the label at time $t$. An
application of the model must state when this idealization is adequate for the
system at hand; for a body whose rotation, deformation or internal structure
matters for the question asked, the point-particle model is not adequate and a
richer model must be specified. The framework makes no claim that every
physical body is a point particle.

**(vii) Calibration caveat.** An apparatus calibration may *estimate* a mass
parameter of a concrete body under a stated measurement model, with its
assumptions, sampling and uncertainty; such an estimate neither defines the
mass parameter of a label nor verifies the equation of motion in which it
occurs, and it is not deduced from this postulate. No measured value of any
mass is asserted by this item.

Let $N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ be given as
in [[post-cm01-worldlines]], and fix one inertial frame of the model with
spatial coordinates $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ for each label $i$. Identify the
space of all position tuples with $\mathbb R^{3N}=(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and
write its points as $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$; each component $x_{i}$ has
dimension $\ell$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an
open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple
$x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to
each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the
**collision set**

$$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$

from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at
coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many
closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map
$x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a
legitimate configuration domain. Whether the exclusion is part of the model is
a modelling decision recorded with the force law; the framework itself only
requires $Q$ to be open and stated.

**(b) Holonomic constraint branch.** Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ be an open
**ambient set**, let $k\in\mathbb N$ with $1\le k\le3N-1$, and let

$$G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{k}):O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k}$$

be a smooth map, each component carrying a declared dimension and unit fixed
by the model (a component can always be rescaled by a nonzero constant without
changing its zero set, and the rescaling is part of the declaration). Assume:

1. **Nonempty level set:** $G^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing$;
2. **Rank condition:** the differential $DG(x):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k}$
   is surjective, equivalently has rank $k$, at every $x\in G^{-1}(0)$.

Then $0$ is a regular value of $G$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]], and the **constrained
configuration space** is $Q:=G^{-1}(0)$. By
[[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] — applied to the smooth
map $G$ from the open subset $O$ of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ to $\mathbb R^{k}$, whose
regular value $0$ has nonempty fibre — $Q$ is an embedded submanifold of
$\mathbb R^{3N}$ of dimension $3N-k$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]).
The **degrees of freedom** of this branch of the model is the number
$$\dim Q=3N-k.$$ In the sense of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]], $Q$ together with the inclusion $X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ is then a particle configuration, and the mass metric of that definition is available with the masses $m_{i}$; the configuration is constrained to $Q$ for all times in this branch.

**(c) Time-dependent holonomic constraints.** If the constraint map depends on
time,

$$G:\mathbb R\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k},\qquad (t,x)\longmapsto G(t,x),$$

with $G$ smooth and $D_{x}G(t_{0},x)$ of rank $k$ at every $x$ of the nonempty
set $G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$, then for each fixed $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$ the
**instantaneous configuration space** $Q_{t_{0}}:=G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$ is an
embedded submanifold of dimension $3N-k$ by the same theorem applied to
$G(t_{0},\cdot)$. The family $\{Q_{t_{0}}\}$ varies with $t_{0}$; a curve
$t\mapsto q(t)$ with $G(t,q(t))=0$ is not thereby a curve in one fixed
manifold, and the kinematic treatment of such constraints (velocities, the
reaction forces that maintain them and the distinction between rheonomic and
scleronomic constraints) belongs to the framework's constraint development and
is not part of this definition.

**(d) Mass operator.** In the ambient coordinates define the **mass operator**
$\mathsf M:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ by block multiplication,

$$\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N});$$

its matrix in the standard basis is block diagonal with blocks $m_{i}I_{3}$,
the **mass matrix** of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]].
Its dimension is $\mu$: it multiplies positions of dimension $\ell$ by masses
of dimension $\mu$. On the constrained branch, for the inclusion
$X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ and tangent vectors $h,z\in T_qQ$,
the mass metric of that item is
$$\mathcal G_q(h,z):=\langle dX_q(h),\mathsf M\,dX_q(z)\rangle_{3N}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_i\,h_i\cdot z_i,$$
where $h_i,z_i\in\mathbb R^3$ are the blocks of $dX_q(h),dX_q(z)$ under
the canonical Euclidean tangent identification specified in that supplier.
It restricts the mass-weighted ambient bilinear form to $T_qQ$, rather than
the unweighted Euclidean inner product.

**(e) Velocity constraints are a different object.** A **velocity-map
constraint** on the open ambient set $O$ is a pair of smooth maps
$$A:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'\times3N},\qquad b:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'},\qquad 1\le k'\le3N,$$
with $A(t,x)$ of constant rank $k'$ everywhere in the declared domain,
imposing $A(t,x(t))\dot x(t)+b(t,x(t))=0$ on a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to O$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval, the parameter $t$ is frame time, and $\dot x(t):=x'(t)$ is the componentwise derivative in the convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Equivalently $A(t,x)$ is a linear map
$\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k'}$. Each row's output unit is declared, and
its corresponding component of $b$ has that same unit. The allowed velocities
at $(t,x)$ form the affine set $\{v:A(t,x)v+b(t,x)=0\}$; its differences form
$\ker A(t,x)$.

The law is **locally holonomic-equivalent at $(t_0,x_0)$** if on some open
neighbourhood $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times O$ of that point there are a $C^2$
map $g:V\to\mathbb R^{k'}$ with $D_xg$ of rank $k'$ and a $C^2$ matrix map
$C:V\to\mathbb R^{k'\times k'}$ with $\det C\ne0$ such that
$$A=C\,D_xg,\qquad b=C\,\partial_tg\qquad\text{on }V.$$
Thus the velocity law is locally the derivative of the regular positional
constraints $g(t,x)=\text{constant}$. It is **locally nonholonomic at the
specified point** when no such neighbourhood and pair $(g,C)$ exists; a
nonholonomic model in this local sense declares a point (or a region of
points) with this failure. For a homogeneous time-independent law this
rules out such a regular-level-set representation throughout a neighbourhood.
It need not rule out an individual embedded submanifold $S\subseteq O$ with
$T_xS=\ker A(x)$ for every $x\in S$, using the ambient tangent identification
of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]]; for an affine
time-dependent law the criterion also includes the drift $b$.
Absence of a single global pair alone does not establish local
nonintegrability. The rank of $A$ counts instantaneous velocity restrictions,
not the dimension of a positional configuration manifold; accessibility
requires its own definition. Rank changes require a separate model.

derivations.claim: The time coordinate and worldline parameter have dimension $[t]=\tau$ and the spatial coordinates $[x_{i}]=\ell$ by the conventions; the dimension of a bilinear product of two quantities is the product of their dimensions, since each component of the product is a sum of products of components to which the rule $[XY]=[X][Y]$ applies.
The coordinate velocity has $[w]=[dx_{\gamma}/dt]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and the coordinate acceleration $[a]=[dw/dt]=\ell\tau^{-2}$, by the derivative rule and step 1.1.

The masses have $[m_{i}]=\mu$, so the mass operator has dimension $\mu$ by [L3]; the momentum $p=mw$ has $[p]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ and the product $m a$ has $[ma]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, both being products of the displayed dimensions.

The frame parameters have the dimensions of [L1]; each law of [L1] is dimensionally consistent: $[t']=[t+b]=\tau$ because $[t]=[b]=\tau$; in $x'=Rx+vt+a_0$ the three summands have dimensions $\ell$, $\ell\tau^{-1}\cdot\tau=\ell$ and $\ell$; $[w']=[Rw+v]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ because $[Rw]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[v]=\ell\tau^{-1}$; and $[a']=[Ra]=\ell\tau^{-2}$.

For the locally specified rotating-basis coordinates $y$ and the angular speed $\omega>0$ measured in radians per second, $[\omega]=\tau^{-1}$ under the radian convention, and the two cross-product expressions are consistent with the acceleration: $[\boldsymbol\omega\times y]=\tau^{-1}\ell=\ell\tau^{-1}=[y']$ and $[\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times y)]=\tau^{-2}\ell=\ell\tau^{-2}=[y'']$, where each component of a cross product is a sum of products of two components, so its dimension is the product of the dimensions.

Finally the locally defined two-particle constraint function has dimension $\ell^{2}$; the level equation $G(x)=0$ relates a quantity of dimension $\ell^{2}$ to the number $0$, which is admissible because $0$ is the neutral element of addition in every dimension, and multiplying $G$ by a nonzero constant of any fixed dimension produces the same zero set with the same ranks of $DG$ on it, as recorded with the definition of the configuration stage; all quantities and laws of this page are therefore dimensionally consistent under the stated conventions.

Let $V$ be a real vector space of dimension $4$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let $\tau:V\to\mathbb R$ be a surjective linear map ([[def-linear-map]]). Put

$$K:=\ker\tau=\{v\in V:\tau(v)=0\},$$

the kernel of $\tau$ ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]). The kernel is a linear subspace ([[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]]), so the quotient vector space $V/K$ is defined ([[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]]). The first isomorphism theorem gives the linear isomorphism $V/K\to\operatorname{im}\tau=\mathbb R$, $v+K\mapsto\tau(v)$ ([[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-for-vector-spaces]]). Since $\mathbb R$ has the one-element standard basis, $\dim\mathbb R=1$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] with $F=\mathbb R$ and $n=1$); rank-nullity for the surjective map $\tau$ therefore gives $\dim K=4-1=3$ ([[thm-rank-nullity]]).

Let $g$ be an inner product on $K$ in the sense of [[def-inner-product-space]]: a symmetric positive definite $\mathbb R$-bilinear form $g:K\times K\to\mathbb R$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set equipped with an action of the additive group of $V$, written $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$, that is free and transitive: explicitly, $(p+v)+w=p+(v+w)$ and $p+0=p$ for all $p\in A$ and $v,w\in V$, and for all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $p+v=q$; write $q-p$ for that unique vector. The identities $p+(q-p)=q$, $(q-p)+(r-q)=r-p$ and $q-p=-(p-q)$ follow from the axioms together with uniqueness of the displacement. Such a set is an **affine space modelled on $V$**, and its elements are **events**. (This formulation restates the affine-space structure used here so that the item is self-contained; the general theory of affine spaces is supplied by the special-relativity collection for its own consumers.)

Fix an orientation of $K$ in the sense of [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]; this is a chosen orientation class, not a chosen spatial basis.

An **adapted chart** for the data $(V,\tau,g,A)$ is a triple $(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ consisting of

1. an origin $o\in A$;
2. a vector $u\in V$ with $\tau(u)=1$;
3. an ordered basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $K$ that is $g$-orthonormal and positively oriented with respect to the fixed orientation of $K$ ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]], [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

An adapted chart exists for every such set of data and fixed orientation, by clause 3 of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]].

For spatial coordinate vectors $x\in\mathbb R^3$, this item uses the one-based labels $x_i:=x(i-1)$ for $1\le i\le3$; thus $(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ lists the values at $0,1,2$ of the function-space vector of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The labels $e_1,e_2,e_3$ name the corresponding ordered spatial basis; they do not change the underlying index set of $\mathbb R^3$.

The **adapted coordinates** of a point $p\in A$ in this chart are the pair $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ determined by

$$p=o+tu+\sum_{i=1}^{3}x_ie_i,$$

when such a pair exists (existence and uniqueness are [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]], so that the notation is defined for every $p$). The number $t$ is the **time coordinate** and $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ the **spatial coordinate vector** of $p$ in the chart. When $K$ is identified with $\mathbb R^3$ through the coordinates in $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, the assignment $p\mapsto(t,x)$ is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$.

**Simultaneous slices.** For $t\in\mathbb R$ set

$$A_t:=\{p\in A:\tau(p-o)=t\}.$$

The family $\{A_t\}_{t\in\mathbb R}$ is the family of **simultaneous slices** of the chart. Each $A_t$ is an affine space modelled on $K$; the derivation is immediate from the affine identities and linearity of $\tau$ and is recorded in [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]]. The **slice distance** of two points $p,q$ in a common slice $A_t$ is

$$d_g(p,q):=\sqrt{g(p-q,\,p-q)},$$

the square root taken in $\mathbb R$; this is defined because $p-q\in K$ for points of a common slice. In adapted coordinates $d_g(p,q)=\|x(p)-x(q)\|_2$, with $\|\cdot\|_2$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about particles and their motion, in the spacetime of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and the frames of [[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Particle labels and worldlines.** A model of the framework has **particle
labels** $i=1,\dots,N$ for some $N\ge1$. To each label and each *inertial
frame* of the model — an adapted chart $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ with
coordinates $(t,x)$ in the sense of [[post-cm01-frames]] — there is assigned a
**worldline** $\gamma_{i}:I\to A$ described in that frame, where
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval — that is, an interval
of the form $(a,b)$ with $-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points —
the curve $\gamma_{i}$ is of class $C^{2}$ in the adapted coordinates of the frame,
and the **parameter condition**

$$\tau\bigl(\gamma_{i}(t)-o\bigr)=t\qquad(t\in I)$$

holds: the curve parameter is the elapsed time from the origin of the frame, so
in the frame's coordinates $\gamma_{i}(t)=(t,x_{i}(t))$ with
$x_{i}:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$. The parameter condition replaces
the causal conditions of relativistic kinematics: no timelike condition on the
velocity and no upper bound on its Euclidean norm is imposed, and the
parameter is not free up to reparametrization.

**(ii) Description in another frame.** The same motion described in a second
inertial frame is the curve obtained by the time reparametrization of the two
frames: if $(t',x')$ are the coordinates of the second frame and
$t'=t+b$ is the time component of the transformation between the two frames
([[post-cm01-frames]], [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]),
then the description of the motion in the second frame is the curve
$\gamma_{i,b}(t'):=\gamma_{i}(t'-b)$, defined on $I+b$, and it again satisfies
the parameter condition $\tau(\gamma_{i,b}(t')-o')=t'$ with respect to the
second frame's origin $o'$. This is a consistency requirement of the model's
frame language; the accompanying spatial transformation of the coordinate
curve is the affine law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]],
and its kinematic consequences are proved in [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(iii) Regularity is frame-independent.** The class of the worldline is
independent of the frame used to describe it: by the transformation law of
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], the coordinates of the
same event in two inertial frames differ by
$t'=t+b$, $x'=Rx+vt+a$ with constant $b,a,v$ and $R\in SO(3)$, so a coordinate
curve is twice continuously differentiable in one inertial frame exactly when
its reparametrized description is twice continuously differentiable in the
other. The assumptions of this postulate are therefore read in any one inertial
frame without loss.

**(iv) Velocity and acceleration.** In a fixed inertial frame the quantities
$w_{i}:=dx_{i}/dt$ and $a_{i}:=d^{2}x_{i}/dt^{2}$ are the **coordinate
velocity** and **coordinate acceleration** of the label, of dimensions
$\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ by [[def-cm01-units]]; they are defined
precisely, and their transformation under a change of inertial frame is
recorded, in [[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]].

**(v) Fixed inertial mass.** Each particle label $i$ carries a **mass**
$m_{i}>0$, a primitive parameter of the model with dimension $\mu$
([[def-cm01-units]]). The mass is fixed: it is the same positive number at all
times and in all inertial frames of this model; the index $i$ identifies a label within that model and asserts no cross-model identification or equality of mass parameters. It
is not a function of the time coordinate, of the position or of the velocity,
and no variable-mass model is a model of this clause. The mass enters the
dynamics only through its later appearance in the equation of motion; this
postulate attaches no dynamics to it. Distinct labels may carry distinct
masses, and the masses are model data, not measured values.

**(vi) Point-particle idealization.** The model retains of each label only its
position and its fixed mass, together with the label index: size, shape, spin,
deformation, temperature and internal degrees of freedom are omitted, and the
quantity $x_{i}(t)$ is the single point representing the label at time $t$. An
application of the model must state when this idealization is adequate for the
system at hand; for a body whose rotation, deformation or internal structure
matters for the question asked, the point-particle model is not adequate and a
richer model must be specified. The framework makes no claim that every
physical body is a point particle.

**(vii) Calibration caveat.** An apparatus calibration may *estimate* a mass
parameter of a concrete body under a stated measurement model, with its
assumptions, sampling and uncertainty; such an estimate neither defines the
mass parameter of a label nor verifies the equation of motion in which it
occurs, and it is not deduced from this postulate. No measured value of any
mass is asserted by this item.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about frames, in the spacetime structure of [[post-cm01-spacetime]].

**(i) Rotations.** A **rotation** is a matrix $R\in SO(3)$, where

$$SO(3)=\left\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3},\ \det R=1\right\}$$

in the sense of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A rotation acts on spatial
column vectors by matrix multiplication; its entries are dimensionless under
the radian convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Rotations are part of the
formulation of spatial changes of basis; the definition of $SO(3)$ itself
asserts nothing about physical space.

**(ii) Inertial frames.** An **inertial frame** is the global adapted affine
chart of the spacetime data determined by

$$o\in A,\qquad u\in V\ \text{with}\ \tau(u)=1,\qquad (e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\ \text{an ordered,}\ g\text{-orthonormal, positively oriented basis of }K,$$

with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ as in [[def-cm-affine-time-space]]: the time
coordinate is $t(p)=\tau(p-o)$ and the spatial coordinates are the coefficients
of $p-o-tu\in K$ in the basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$. Existence and uniqueness
of the coordinates, and the affine structure of the slices, are the mathematical
content of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]] and
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]]; no physical claim beyond the reading of clause
(iii) is attached to them here.

An inertial frame is a **coordinate chart**: the triple $(o,u,(e_{i}))$. It is
definitively not an observer congruence and not a time-varying basis field. In
the model the basis $(e_{i})$ is fixed once and for all; a family of bases
depending on the time coordinate is a different structure, whose kinematics is
defined separately where it is used, and is not an inertial frame. The physical
reading of the frame is that $t$ is the model's time coordinate in seconds and
$x$ the spatial position in metres, by the conventions of
[[def-cm01-units]].

**(iii) Stationary observers.** For $x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ the curve
$\alpha_{x_{0}}:\mathbb R\to A$, $\alpha_{x_{0}}(t):=o+tu+\sum_{j=1}^{3}(x_{0})_{j}e_{j}$,
is the **observer at rest in the frame at position $x_{0}$**; the family
$\{\alpha_{x_{0}}\}_{x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}}$ is the **stationary observer
congruence** of the frame. Each curve has $t(\alpha_{x_{0}}(s))=s$, is
$C^{\infty}$ in adapted coordinates, and in the frame's own spatial
coordinates has constant coordinate triple $x_{0}$. Here an **observer
worldline** means precisely a $C^2$ curve $\alpha:I\to A$ on a nondegenerate
open real interval with $t(\alpha(s))=s$, used to describe an observer; the
stationary curves just defined have $I=\mathbb R$. This kinematic definition
assigns neither a particle label nor a mass or a dynamical law to an observer.
A particle worldline will separately be assigned to a particle label in the
particle postulate. The congruence is a derived object, determined by the frame and the spacetime data, not an additional primitive. Distinct frames can have the same family of parametrized curves: if $o' = o+\sum_jc_je_j$ while $u'=u$ and $e_j'=e_j$, then $\alpha'_{x_0}(t)=\alpha_{x_0+c}(t)$ for all $t$. Thus shifting only the spatial origin relabels this family. Changing $u$ changes the curve family, since every curve in it has the affine derivative $u$.

**(iv) Allowed changes between frames.** The model adopts the class of
transformations between inertial frames

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x'=Rx+vt+a,$$

where $b\in\mathbb R$ is a **time shift** ($[b]=\tau$), $a\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a
**spatial translation** ($[a_{i}]=\ell$), $v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a **boost
velocity** ($[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$) and $R\in SO(3)$ a **rotation**
($[R_{ij}]=1$). Every pair of inertial frames is related by exactly one such
transformation: that two adapted charts of the same data differ by a
transformation of this form, with $R\in SO(3)$ because both bases are
positively oriented, is the mathematical transformation law proved in
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]. Uniqueness follows by comparing the coordinate maps on all $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$: evaluating the time map fixes $b$; evaluating the spatial map at $(0,0)$ fixes $a$, at $(1,0)$ fixes $v$, and at $(0,e_j)$ for the three standard coordinate vectors fixes each column of $R$. The kinematic
consequences of the law — the transformation of coordinate velocity and
acceleration, and the frame-independence of zero coordinate acceleration — are
proved as a statement about the model in
[[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(v) Free motion is not asserted here.** The framework's dynamics enters
through the force and equation-of-motion postulates of the pages that follow;
those pages adopt, as the content of Newton's first law, that there exist
inertial frames in the sense of clause (ii) in which a particle with zero
applied interaction has zero coordinate acceleration. This postulate
introduces the frames and their changes but asserts no dynamics: it does not
state that any particular motion has zero acceleration, and it does not
privilege any one inertial frame — each of them is a legitimate arena for the
formulation of the model's equations.

**(vi) Kinematic symmetry is not conservation.** The class (iv) is a class of
coordinate changes. A quantity is **conserved along a motion** when its value as a function of the frame time is constant on the interval of that motion. No such constancy is asserted here, nor is it asserted that every
mechanical system's description is invariant in form; a force law must also
transform appropriately under (iv) to be a law of the model in every frame, and
an external apparatus or background field can single out frames for the
description of a concrete experiment. Conservation statements, when they hold,
are theorems of later pages with their own hypotheses, not consequences of
this postulate.

Let $(V,\tau,g,A)$ be as in [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] and let $(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ and $(o',u',(e_1',e_2',e_3'))$ be two adapted charts, with coordinate functions $(t,x)$ and $(t',x')$ of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]].

1. There are $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,v\in\mathbb R^3$ and a matrix $R\in O(3)$ such that for every $p\in A$

$$t'(p)=t(p)+b,\qquad x'(p)=R\,x(p)+v\,t(p)+a.$$

If $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(e_1',e_2',e_3')$ are both positively oriented for the fixed orientation of $K$, then $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]).

2. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be a map whose first-chart time coordinate satisfies $t(\gamma(s))=s$ for all $s\in I$. Write $x(s):=x(\gamma(s))$ and $y(s):=x'(\gamma(s))$. The regularity hypothesis below means that this coordinate function $x:I\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuously differentiable (respectively, twice continuously differentiable); no additional smooth structure on $A$ is assumed. If $x$ is continuously differentiable then $y$ is continuously differentiable with

$$y'(s)=R\,x'(s)+v\qquad(s\in I),$$

and if $x$ is twice continuously differentiable then $y''(s)=R\,x''(s)$ for all $s\in I$. Equivalently, in the differentiated variables of the two charts, $dx'/dt'=R\,dx/dt+v$ and $d^2x'/dt'^2=R\,d^2x/dt^2$.

3. Consequently $x''=0$ on $I$ if and only if $y''=0$ on $I$: the two charts agree on which time-parametrized curves have zero coordinate acceleration.

derivations.claim: The standard chart is adapted and its coordinates are the standard ones: $o=0$, $u=(1,0,0,0)$ has $\tau(u)=1$, the standard basis is orthonormal and positively oriented, and for $p=(x^{0},x^{1},x^{2},x^{3})$ the expansion $p=o+x^{0}u+\sum_{j}x^{j}e_{j}$ exhibits the adapted coordinates as $t=x^{0}$, $x=(x^{1},x^{2},x^{3})$ by [L1]. The assigned curve $\gamma(t)=tu$ is $C^{\infty}$ on $\mathbb R$, has $F$-coordinates $(t,0,0,0)$ and satisfies $\tau(\gamma(s)-o)=s$. Thus its assignment to label $1$ with the specified fixed positive mass satisfies [L2]; worldline status uses that assignment, not the parameter condition alone.

The curve $\kappa(s)=2su$ has $\tau(\kappa(s)-o)=2s$, which differs from $s$ for every $s\ne0$, for instance at $s=1$ the value is $2$; therefore $\kappa$ **fails** the parameter condition and is not a worldline of the model, although it is of class $C^{\infty}$ and its image is the same time axis as that of $\gamma$; it is the reparametrization $\kappa(s)=\gamma(2s)$. The parameter condition is thus a genuine restriction, and the image of a curve does not determine whether it is a worldline.

Under a change of frame the parameter condition is consistent with the reparametrization: by [L3] the same worldline $\gamma$ satisfies $t'(\gamma(s))=s+b$, so the curve $\gamma_{b}(t'):=\gamma(t'-b)$, defined on the shifted interval, satisfies $t'(\gamma_{b}(t'))=t'$ and is the description of the motion in $F'$ in the sense of [L2]; the time shift $b$ is absorbed into the reparametrization. For the explicit worldline of step 1.1 this reads $\gamma_{b}(t')=(t'-b)u$.

For the affine reparametrizations in one fixed frame, $\tau(\kappa_{\lambda,\mu}(s)-o)=t(\gamma(\lambda s+\mu))=\lambda s+\mu$ by [L1] and step 1.1, and the equation $\lambda s+\mu=s$ holds for all real $s$ exactly when $\lambda=1$ and $\mu=0$. Hence no nontrivial affine reparametrization preserves the parameter condition in a fixed frame: the parameter of a worldline is fixed to be the frame time, and a reparametrized curve with $\lambda\ne1$ becomes a worldline only after the inverse reparametrization. The example confirms that both the parameter and the frame enter the definition of a worldline, as recorded in [L2].
